The House resumed from Thursday, October 31 consideration of the motion of Miss MacDonald that Bill C-62, an Act respecting Employment Equity, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee, and on the amendment of Mr. Keeper (p. 8197).
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, this will be the last day of debate on Bill C-62 at second reading. The Government for the fifth time in this session of Parliament has imposed closure, cut off debate, on an important Government Bill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: Something you never used to do, did you?
Oh, oh!

As a result of that procedure by the Government, we are not permitted to have a full discussion in this House of what is supposed to be one of the key pieces of legislation put forward by the Government.
The Government has made a lot, both in the Speech from the Throne and in speeches that have followed, about the reform of Parliament. The Government established a committee, headed by the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), to examine the rules of Parliament and to suggest ways in which Parliament can be reformed to give Members on both sides of the House the opportunity for more input into legislation so that legislation will not be formulated in the back rooms of the civil service. In other words, those who are elected to this House will have some say in the drafting, in the amendment and in the content of legislation.
If the Government continues to use allocation of time and continues to cut off debate on Bills so Members of Parliament cannot have that input, what does that say about reform of Paliament? It says that the Government is not really serious about reform of Parliament. The proposals put forward are simply a facade and not a real approach to parliamentary affairs.
When we debate an issue in Parliament, such as we want to do with this Bill on employment equity, we know that we are not going to convince too many of the 211 Conservative Members on the other side to change their minds. We know that there are only 70 of us in opposition, 40 in one Party and 30 in another and despite the soundness of our arguments, we will not convince too many Conservatives to change their minds.
The purpose of debate in this House-and this does not begin with this Parliament-is to reach beyond the walls of Parliament to the public outside where we hope to touch public opinion. If we touch public opinion by continuing the debate in this House, through the media and through those who may watch the proceedings of Parliament, then pressure may be put on the Government and the Government will begin to amend and withdraw Bills. That is what happened when we dealt with the proposal to cut back indexation of old age pensions. If it had been for the government caucus itself, deindexation would have proceeded, but by debate in this House and outside the House the public became aware of what was happening to old age pensions. The public went after the Government. The 211 Member majority responded to the mass of public opinion that was brought to bear on the Government to amend and draw back on that proposal. We believe the debate should continue on this Bill. We abhor the fact that the Government is cutting off debate on Bill C-62 and that this is the last day on second reading.
Why do we oppose this Bill and why are we trying to make the public aware of what is happening? This Bill pretends, and I say pretends, to do something about employment equity. Employment equity is supposed to bring about fairer conditions of employment for certain target groups who have had a rough deal generation after generation. I am speaking of the women, the visible minorities, our native people and the handicapped. This Bill pretends to do something about those particular groups in our population so that they will have a fairer deal in seeking and maintaining employment.
The Bill was supposed to be based upon the recommendations of the Abella Report. The previous Government appointed Judge Abella in 1983 to look into the whole problem of inequity in the employment market-place and to make recommendations on how it could be corrected. Judge Abella tabled her report in November, 1984, after the change of Government, making some very specific recommendations on what must be done. Unfortunately, the Government has not followed those recommendations.

November 21, 1985
Employment Equity
We are opposing the Bill because while it expresses the right intent-it indicates that it wants to do something about the situation of inequity in the employment market-place for different target groups in our population-it in fact does very little. There are no standards set out in the Bill. There are no objective criteria which must be followed. There is no enforcement agency set out in the Bill. In fact, there are no penalties if the employers who are subject to the Bill do not follow through with what is expected of them. The only penalty in the Bill is for employers who do not report to the Government. However, if they report, and even if their reports are wanting or are lacking in progress, there is no penalty. The only penalty is if they do not report.
Judge Abella, in her report, demanded that there be an enforcement agency, standards and penalties. The Bill does not provide for them. This is why we are opposing it and trying to make clear to Canadians that while the Bill pretends to do something, it does very little. We are afraid that if the Bill passes, the Government can then say that it has done something about employment equity, when in fact it will have done nothing at all and will go on pretending that something meaningful has been done. If the Government really wanted to do something, it would have put into law what Judge Abella recommended.
I am not the only one who says this. The great mass of public opinion is not yet aware of the faqade which is going on here. However, the leaders of the target groups do. They have come to Ottawa, have visited our offices and have told us so. The leaders of the handicapped associations have told us that the Bill is not acceptable. Also they have told us that they would rather see it defeated than passed in this half measure form before us. Women's groups have come to Ottawa, such as the National Action Committee and other organizations, and have told us that the Bill is not acceptable. The leaders of visible minorities and native people have told us that the Bill is not acceptable. Yet, the Minister and Members on the Government side tell us what a great Bill it is.
The Bill is not to serve most of us in the House of Commons; it is to serve those people who are considered target groups under the Bill. If they do not think it is acceptable, why does the Government not do what we have asked, take back the Bill and make some amendments to it?
The Bill could be improved and could be made worth while, if key amendments were made to it. I am afraid those key amendments cannot be made in committee. At first I thought they could be made after the Bill was sent to committee on second reading, that that would do the job. Now, after further consideration, I have come to the conclusion that the Bill is so defective and needs so many amendments that it should be sent back to the drawing-board. The Government should reform the Bill, revise the Bill and bring it back to us. Then it would be doing something to please those target groups.
One wonders who the Government is trying to please with the Bill. Rather than trying to meet the needs of the groups to which I have referred, those who have difficulty with employment-women, native people, the handicapped and visible
minorities-it is really backing off Judge Abella's recommendations because it does not want to offend big business which does not want too much regulation or interference with its employment practices.
The decision in the Bill as to what the standards should be is left to the employers. That is really surprising. It is a very unusual situation. A Bill will be passed which indicates that employers must do something about a certain problem, in this case employment inequity, but the Government leaves it up to them to decide what the standards will be. That is what the Government is doing in Clause 4 which reads:
An employer shall implement employment equity by
(a) identifying and eliminating each of the employer's employment practices,
not otherwise authorized by a law, that results in employment barriers against
persons in designated groups-
It is saying to the employers that they decide which of their practices are against employment equity and do something about them. How many employers will say that they have been doing the wrong thing for several years and now they will make changes in some of their policies? We need standards in the Bill. We need an enforcement agency. I hope the Government does something about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
The Hon. Member might be right.
It is with considerable pleasure that I am able to rise today to endorse the historic Bill which my colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), presented some time ago. All Members of the House must recognize that we have reached a landmark, no matter what imperfections might be perceived, with this Bill. That focus should be kept on most of the discussions because in many of these things there are always matters which could be done better or could be done different. There is no particular Bill, no particular passage of literature, which contains all the wisdom. However, the House should not miss the point; it is a landmark Bill.
With the passage of the Canadian Human Rights Act of 1977 and the proclamation of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms in 1983, the people of the country clearly stated that employment discrimination could no longer be tolerated in a democratic society. With the passage of the Employment Equity Act, we will ensure that employers, both public and
November 21, 1985

private, will be responsible to ensure that equality becomes a reality.
Over the past 14 months, it has been my pleasure to criss-cross the country, talking with native people. After visiting many communities, hundreds of communities, I can say that few issues have dominated my discussions as much as the desire on the part of native people for economic development and employment. With unemployment rates reaching 80 per cent in many communities, native people want the opportunity for long-term productive employment. They want the types of jobs which will allow them to break out of the dependency relationships which they see as a major threat to the survival of their own culture and communities. Few other Canadians face the kind of barriers to employment which Indian people face. For many, there is a need to upgrade their education, to acquire occupational skills through training, and to obtain work experience and the special assistance necessary to enter the labour market successfully.
Recently I was pleased to announce the Indian Community Human Resource Strategies Program. It is designed to provide resources to Indian communities in order that they can provide their members with the skills, experience and other assistance the world of work increasingly requires. However, all the training and preparation in the world will be a waste if Indian people do not have opportunities for employment at whatever job and at whatever level for which they are qualified. Whether intentional or unintentional-and native workers are often excluded because of invalid or inappropriate employment requirements-discriminatory barriers for native people must be removed. Even further, employers must be prepared to demonstrate to potential Indian employees that those opportunities are there. Again, the figures are compelling. If Indian people are to reach the same employment levels as other Canadians by the 1991 census, some 85,000 jobs must be created just to get close to the level of other Canadians.
Certainly, our Government is committed to assisting Indian communities and individuals to develop fully the employment opportunities on reserves. However, even with success, a minimum of 60 per cent to 70 per cent of the required jobs will have to be in the non-Indian private and public sectors. Clearly, whether they are opportunities for Indian workers commuting from the reserve or for those choosing to live off the reserve, we must be prepared to ensure finally that Indians will have a fair share access to employment in this country.
I am convinced that this Bill represents the cornerstone of its successful employment strategy for native Canadians. Despite the rhetoric we sometimes hear from the other side, as it is part of their job, employers as defined in this Act will be required-I emphasize required-to implement employment equity. First, they will be required to remove all barriers which discriminate against designated groups, whether intentional or systemic. Second, they will be required to implement positive measures to ensure an appropriate degree of representation. Third, they will be required to provide annual reports to the
Employment Equity
Minister of Employment and Immigration on exactly how well they are doing with respect to achieving employment equity.
There are those who would criticize the Bill because it establishes no new enforcement agency. However, the facts show something different. Crown corporations will be required to submit mandatory employment equity plans to Treasury Board and will be closely monitored for compliance. Federal contractors will be required by law to certify their commitment to implement employment equity and they will be monitored. Those failing to comply will face debarrment, and that is a very powerful incentive. Companies under federal jurisdiction will be required, under penalty of a stiff fine, to report publicly their employment data on a yearly basis. If they make no progress, Section 32(3) of the Canadian Human Rights Act clearly gives the Human Rights Commission the right to initiate complaints with respect to it. For the first time, the commission will have the information required to monitor employment practices.
As my colleague stated earlier, the Government is also committed to ensuring that the commission has the staff and resources to carry out that part of the mandate. If this Bill does not have a new enforcement agency it is because the Government believes in using the powers of the agencies already in place. What we do not need is another redundant agency. We need the action that this Bill gives to those people who are looking for employment equity. Officials in my Department are currently working with over 80 Indian communities which are negotiating with Crown corporations and private employers for employment opportunities. This long list includes oil and gas, transportation and service industries and construction companies. Many other communities will be developing and implementing long-term human resource plans as part of our human resources strategies program.
I can assure all Members that the employment equity program will be an enormous boost in all of these communities. It will help pry open doors that have long been closed to Indian people. The prospects are exciting for them. It is historic and I believe that all Members of the House should support this Bill.
Nothing in the world is perfect, but I can say that this Bill moves this country forward such a distance that it will make all Hon. Members who support this Bill proud they did so and those who do not will wonder why.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to Bill C-62, I am pleased to have the opportunity to follow the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie). As the Minister is well aware, the native population in my riding is approximately 30 per cent of the total. We have had experience in the past with provincial regulation that is very similar to the Bill before us today. Therefore, I am aware of the difficulties we will face in turning this Bill into a real affirmative action program. The intent of the employment equity Bill must be to provide real equity and real participation at all levels in the workforce for

November 21, 1985
Employment Equity
those disadvantaged groups, whether they are native people, women, the handicapped or others.
During my term as Public Service critic for my caucus prior to the last election, I read many reports stating that there was no real equity within the structure of the federal Public Service. The problems have not been resolved after many years of Liberal study and after a year of Conservative promises. I believe we will suffer from the same inefficiencies as a result of this Bill.
During the election campaign the Government promised to implement mandatory affirmative action. Again, this promise is being broken by this legislation.
Let me explain why 1 believe this legislation is flawed and will not fulfil the task that it should. Large hydro development projects were being implemented in Manitoba during the 1970s. At that time a northern preference clause was negotiated with the contractors and sub-contractors who were involved in these large projects that employed thousands of people. However, there was essentially no enforcement mechanism or method of ensuring that native people and women really became involved in the process. We have learned from those negotiations in the 1970s, and as we gear up for new projects in Manitoba at Limestone and Conawapa, we have built in quotas and indicated that various trades must provide up to 45 per cent native hiring and maintain 45 per cent native employment in some trades on those projects. There must be training for those people before the projects begin in order for them to be qualified for the jobs as they come on stream. In this case, I will give credit to the federal Government for helping to pay for these training projects. In particular, I give credit to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) for agreeing with the Manitoba Government to pay for some of the training that is involved in that project.
However, this illustrates that there must be some real enforcement mechanism provided in this Bill. It is not enough to leave it up to the companies to look after their own affairs and simply report to the Government. We have had experience with years and years of reports about the federal civil service. We know that women are under-represented and we know, as the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is well aware, that native people are under-represented especially in areas where they live. We know that the higher one goes in the hierarchy, the fewer disadvantaged people there are, fewer women and fewer native people employed in the Government. While that information is useful in itself, the process must continue to achieve the goal of real equity. That is what we are looking at in this legislation. It is unfortunate but true that this Bill is only a step along the road to what we need.
I would like to see the Government live up to its election promise of mandatory affirmative action for corporations that are involved in very large Government contracts. That was a promise, and presumably a promise is made to be kept. However, it is not being kept.
The fact that almost every major Canadian organization that is concerned about women, natives and the handicapped have spoken out against this legislation, tells us a great deal. They have said that it is not adequate and is not in keeping with the promise the Government made during the election campaign. There is really no enforcement mechanism that will make sure anything will really happen as a result of this legislation. There is no guarantee that these corporations will even fill out the forms the Government will produce for them.
As the labour spokesperson for our Party, I am concerned about the fact that there is no provision for the input of unions in this legislation. Unions are the ones that are involved in negotiating and it is their members who are affected. The unions could have input in terms of educational leave for purposes of helping people move up the ladder within the company. Yet there is no input from the unions suggested in this legislation. A Government that has prided itself on its consultation is leaving out a very fundamental group which has a lot of input into what will happen in the workplace. Again, this legislation is flawed because of that lack.
As well, this legislation is flawed because it lacks not only the goals but the guidelines for affirmative action. What does the Government expect to happen as a result of this legislation next year, two years down the road or five years from now? I think we have a right to know that. Year after year we have seen a failure within the federal civil service to deal with real affirmative action. I have talked about the fact that there has been study after study and that chart after chart has been shown to us. What is the real goal of the federal Government with regard to its own employees? We are talking about hundreds of thousands of Canadians. What are the goals of the Government with regard to Crown corporations? What are the Government's goals and expectations for the effect of this legislation on the private sector? I think we should know that and I think that is the problem we are facing at this time.
We are dealing with a piece of legislation which I do not believe will do very much for the people about whom we are so concerned. I think that in 1985, the people have a right to expect more than a piece of legislation which would have been found to be faulty even in the 1960s and the 1970s. The Government is moving in the right direction. There is no question about that. However, I think that it is moving very slowly and probably very cautiously, which is certainly not in keeping with the bold statements made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) during the election campaign.
I have lived in northern Manitoba and seen mining companies bring in workforces from outside. I have seen other companies bring their workforces with them to the North. Because of that, I recognize that voluntary plans do not often work. Sure, we can say that we are open to native hiring and the advancement of women. However, if we are not going to do anything about it, that will not help the situation.
I do not think that INCO in Thompson had any particular regulation indicating that native people could not be hired but the net result was that very few native people were hired. It was only in cases like the one of Sherritt Gordon for which the
November 21, 1985

Government had specific programs that native people were actually being hired. It was only for Manfor Ltd. that the Government made specific regulations and developed hiring programs so native people would be employed in the forestry industry.
In closing, because we are under time allocation and I am limited to speaking only 10 minutes, I would say that the legislation is too weak. I can certainly speak from the experience I have had in my own riding and I say that it ain't going to work.

Mr. Speaker, I too am rather concerned and disappointed that the Government is bringing a halt to debate on this very important employment equity Bill. A lot more needs to be said on this issue. Frankly, a lot of the things that have been said already need to be said again, because it is obvious that the Government is not listening.
I do not think anyone on this side of the House is quarrelling with the Bill per se. It is just that the Bill does not do what the Government said it was going to do. It certainly will not do what the Abella Royal Commission wanted done in this regard. This Bill provides us in the House of Commons with a chance to do something for women, visible minorities, native people and the disabled in the workplace. This is the moment when we can achieve something for these groups. If we let this opportunity go by with just a cursory glance, we may not get another chance, with the thinking of this Government, for some time to come. We have to be cognizant of the importance of this Bill, particularly at this time when we have before us this legislation and we can do something regarding this very important matter.
This Bill, as has been stated by the affected groups, just does not go far enough. This is the tragedy. It indicates to me that the Government is not sincere in what it is attempting to have the Canadian people believe. We in Canada made a good start with the Canadian Human Rights Act of 1977, with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and particularly with Article 15 of the Charter. It was hoped that this Bill would provide the additional buoyancy that would support these groups in their attempt to attain what the Government should be giving to them.
There are a few things about the Bill with which I would like to deal. As has been mentioned, the definition of employer in the Bill is any person who employs 100 or more employees on or in connection with federal work undertaken. That is just not sufficient. There are holes in that definition through which one could drive a truck. It is not a clause that would be designed by a Government that wants to put teeth and feeling into the stated purpose of this Bill, a very important matter for these groups.
Clause 4 refers to identifying and eliminating each of the employer's employment practices not otherwise authorized by law. If it were not so obvious, we would say that the Government was just being naive. To try to give an objective standard to the subjective position of employers and leaving it at that is
Employment Equity
far from being sufficient. In fact, it is bordering on being insulting to the intelligence of the Canadian people and particularly the groups that we on this side of the House wish to help, the groups that the Government is not helping anywhere near to the extent that is needed.
I listened to the Hon. Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie). He made some very good points, points which I think all Canadians should consider regarding the seriousness of native employment. I think the Minister mentioned that we need to create 85,000 jobs by 1991 if we are going to bring native people anywhere close to the norm of employment levels in Canada. It is astounding for a country with the prosperity and enlightenment of Canada to have our native people in that type of position. Something has to be done, something more than what we see in this Bill.
I am not only distressed by the fact that the Bill does not carry the strength which is needed to protect native people and to secure employment for them, but I am distressed by the Government's policy with respect to abandoning its regional development aspect. I know that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall), will say more about this when he speaks. At least when we had a Department of Regional Industrial Expansion we had a way to help those people who were no longer on the reserve to work hand in hand with the work which was being done by the Minister responsible for the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Those natives who are no longer on the reserve have no way of being assisted by the Government. The Bill does not go far enough in that regard.
As has been said earlier, there are no teeth in the Bill. There are no sanctions. There is certainly provision for a fine of up to $5,000 if companies do not report on their progress and position with respect to the requirements of the Bill. However, it is not enough to have these targeted companies and organizations do what we want them to do to enforce the principle, purpose and heart of the Bill.
The Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) said that he does not know what the goals of the Bill are. The Government is not saying what the goals are, that is true. I think we can see a clear indication of what the goals of the Government are when it says that even though it requires a report and the sanction applies only to a report not being filed, it does not have to be filed until June 1, 1988. The Government is obviously not expecting anything from the Bill and from the targeted organizations and companies until after June 1, 1988. Without the spirit of accomplishing what the Government says it wants to accomplish, the Bill will not go anywhere near achieving what we want to achieve and what the Canadian people want to achieve. As has been said earlier, Canadians do not want a continuance of this discrimination. That is becoming more and more obvious.
The Bill will just not do anything. The recommendations of the special committee dealing with the handicapped have been pretty well discounted. The Abella Commission said that the

November 21, 1985
Employment Equity
recommendations in the report entitled Obstacles have to be followed in a Bill such as this if it is to have meaningful application. That has not been done. The recommendations of the Abella Commission have not been followed. What we have is smoke and mirrors with respect to this very important question. Visible minorities, the handicapped, native people and the disabled have been waiting a long time. When I say a long time 1 mean that something should have been done a long time ago. What I am afraid of is that by having this insufficient Bill become law people will say: "Oh well, this question has been looked after and the needs of these groups have been looked after". It just ain't necessarily so. It will not happen. This Bill is not the answer. It has to be strengthened. We can no more abandon the search for the just practice and treatment of these groups after the passage of this Bill than we could before it was introduced.
I am concerned that there will be no follow-up and that companies will look at this legislation as just another porous document to which they will give only cursory glances now and again. Without any of the principles which we in the Liberal Party want to see but in the Bill these aims will not be put into practice. I think that will be very unfortunate.
I ask the Government to reconsider this Bill and to look at it again. I ask the Government to give further consideration to strengthening the Bill. The Government should listen to Hon. Members on this side of the House, put some teeth into the Bill and do what it says it wants done in Clause 2.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to speak in support of Bill C-62, an Act respecting employment equity. For years the Liberal Government paid lip service to the doctrine of equal opportunity in the workplace. It was all talk and no action. With its strong mandate from the people of Canada the present Government has given this basic right top priority. In fact, within our first year in office we have drafted a Bill which will finally make employment equity a reality. Members opposite are still all talk and no action.
We have had enough, as have the Canadian people. Women, native people, disabled persons and visible minorities want to see some action. They want to see results. They demand legislation which will enshrine the right of all Canadians, not just the white, able-bodied males, equal access to employment opportunities. They have waited patiently through years of rhetoric and self-serving inaction. However, with the Bill which is before us now the barriers are coming down. We have shared their frustration and we have heard their cries. As legislators we are committed to opening wide the doors of opportunity for all Canadians.
Not only will the doors be opened but here is the clout of this legislation. Employers will be held accountable for implementing special measures to ensure a truly representative workforce. Critics say the Bill is not tough enough. They say that accountability is not mandatory, that business will not comply and that employers will fudge their reports. This attitude of mistrust and confrontation toward the business community is counter-productive. I might say that this is one
of the reasons the labour market and, indeed, the economy as a whole was in the sorry state in which we found it when we assumed power.
I am proud to say that my Government has confidence in the integrity and intelligence of the business community and that, when required by law to report annually on the status of designated groups in the organization, they will comply, both through social conscience and because it makes good business sense. I am convinced they will comply because we are giving them clear guidelines and a firm but realistic deadline.
All employers within the federal jurisdiction must begin immediately to examine their employment procedures and to explore remedies to unfair practices. Systems must be established so that data can be collected to support an annual report on the status of designated groups beginning in 1988.
Recognizing that there are always a few bad apples and not, as some would have us think, that the whole barrel is bad, a fine of up to $50,000 will be levied if a report is not submitted or if it is incomplete. If real progress in the elimination of barriers is not substantiated, the report will be open to public and media scrutiny and it will be made subject to the full force of the Canadian Human Rights Commission.
As can be seen, we mean business. We are determined to liberate victims of past discrimination, but as you can also see, Mr. Speaker, we believe in co-operation rather than confrontation to persuade business to conform. We know it is made up of, for the most part, responsible corporate citizens. We also know they are not fools. They are vulnerable to public opinion and they respect the bottom line.
Business sets goals and timetables for every aspect of its operations; profits, capital investment and productivity increases. Setting goals and timetables for designated minorities is a way of ensuring and measuring progress. I think most companies are aware as well that they can no longer afford to waste the potential contribution of capable people for artificial reasons. What is more, the Canadian companies which are already applying the principles of employment equity such as Nova and the Royal Bank, find that their efforts to hire and promote designated groups have resulted in increased productivity, reduced recruitment and training costs, together with a more appropriate use of human resources.
Employment equity makes good business sense. It also enhances the corporate image. If employees, including women, native people, disabled persons and designated minorities are offered equal opportunities, there is a noticeable increase in job satisfaction and morale. Does this improved morale and productivity shine through to the customer and to the public? Yes, it does. Everyone is a potential employee. Everyone is a potential customer. Any company with a representative workforce has something of which to be proud.
The purpose of employment equity legislation is to ensure that all Canadians, particularly victims of past discrimination, can stand proud and confident that in Canada people are hired
November 21, 1985

and promoted according to only one criterion, the ability to do the job.

Mr. Speaker, I also want to join in this debate on Bill C-62, an Act respecting employment equity. I think we should ask ourselves why the Government has chosen to bring in closure on this particular piece of legislation. This is the fifth occasion, I believe, that the Government has brought in closure on a piece of legislation which it has deemed to be important to all Canadians. Why, then, the rush? Why does the Government want to choke off debate on this particular subject matter? Why the hurry, Mr. Speaker? Would it have to do with the contents of Bill C-62?
If we examine Bill C-62 we see that the phrase "designated groups" means women, aboriginal peoples, persons with disabilities and persons who belong to a visible minority. That is what the Bill directs itself to. I believe, as the Elon. Member for Calgary South (Mrs. Sparrow) indicated, that it is an important piece of legislation, but when we look at the substance of the Bill, the four and a half pages-two and a half of which are legalese which is included in every piece of legislation which comes before Parliament-we see, perhaps, a page and a half which somehow addresses itself to the issue of employment equity. The Bill does not address the issues affecting those individuals and those groups of whom I have made mention; women, aboriginal peoples, persons with disabilities and visible minorities. The Government is bringing in closure on this Bill for the simple reason, I suggest, that it has very little to offer women, aboriginal peoples, persons with disabilities or, indeed, individuals who belong to visible minority groups. The Bill is totally lacking in substance and in enforcement procedure to ensure that equality is brought to bear in the workplace. Clause 7 of Bill C-62 reads, and I quote:
The Minister shall in each year prepare a consolidation of the reports received in that year under section 5 and shall, as soon as possible thereafter but not later than the end of that year, cause the consolidation,... to be laid before each House of Parliament.
We are going to have to wait until after the next federal election-which is 31 months from now-before reports are tabled with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald). Then we have to wait for the end of the calendar year before the Minister tables her reports. That is a considerable length of time. The Government promised the Canadian people that if it was elected it would take strong initiatives in order to see that employment equity was brought to the workplace. It is certainly not living up to its election promises, nor is it living up to the comments made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration that this subject matter in itself is important. It will take 31 months before companies in this country submit their reports to the federal Minister, and thereafter we will have to wait until the end of the calendar year before they are tabled before Parliament.
What about an enforcement agency for breaches of this particular piece of legislation, Mr. Speaker? What about the sanctions for not complying with the legislation? Where are
Employment Equity
the standards? Where do we want to be on June 1, 1988, with respect to the provisions of this Bill? Has there been any statement of any goals or objectives set out by the Minister involved? There has been nothing. All we have is two or three pieces of paper about a subject matter which is important to all Canadians. The Government says it is concerned-as Clause 2 states-"to achieve equality in the workplace". But it takes more than pious statements by Ministers or Members of Parliament to achieve the goal of equality in the workplace. And sometimes measures may have to be taken, unfortunate as it may be, to call to task certain corporations and individuals with respect to seeing that equality is restored to the workplace. However, this Bill says nothing. It gives women, native people, the disabled and visible minorities nothing. These people may have to wait for 31 months and longer before Parliament will see the reports. In other words, the wrongs will not be righted by this legislation. These wrongs will continue and there will be no check for more than 31 months.
I had hoped Government Members would be a little more forthcoming in setting out the goals and objectives to be reached at the end of 31 months, but they have not been. I had hoped that the Government would provide clear and unequivocal sanctions in the Bill for those who breached its provisions in the workplace. That has not been the case. Then, to add insult to injury, the Government is using the guillotine, as Members opposite often referred to it when they were in opposition, to cut off debate on this very important matter. That is a shameful thing for a Government elected by the Canadian people en masse on the promise, among others, of substantive changes regarding equality in the workplace.
What do we have to show for it? A smoke and mirrors campaign by the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the Prime Minister of Canada. That is not what Canadians need. That is why groups from coast to coast have denounced the substance of this legislation. Surely in 1985 women, native people, the disabled and visible minorities have legal rights. Surely we, as Members of Parliament, have to give them our support in making sure that those rights are observed and that equality is brought to the workplace.
In closing, I suggest that this Bill ought to be withdrawn by the Government and replaced with legislation with substance, sanctions, enforcement ability and time restrictions on compliance.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill C-62, and in particular on our motion for a six-month delay on second reading. It is strange for an NDP Member to be asking that the Government and Parliament not deal with this Bill immediately. We have been prodding the Government to bring in employment equity legislation for a very long time. However, the sad fact is that this legislation is totally inadequate and we do not want to see it pass. We will be voting against it because of its very serious inadequacies. We would like the Government to spend the next six months in taking a real hard look at the problem and then

November 21, 1985
Employment Equity
come back with some legislative proposals adequate to meet the needs of Canadians who suffer discrimination in the workplace, Canadians who are disadvantaged and who expect some action on the problem by the Government.
One thing the Government could do in the next six months is look at the Abella Report entitled Equality in Employment. It has a substantial list of recommendations on dealing with the employment discrimination that women, visible minorities, native persons and the disabled experience in Canada. In the section dealing with voluntary versus mandatory measures, which is absolutely crucial because it is the lack of mandatory measures which make this Bill unfit to be passed, it says:
Voluntary employment equity means that employers are encouraged, rather than required, to adopt measures intended to rectify employment inequities. There is no provision for an enforcement component. A voluntary program with a mandatory reporting requirement is nonetheless voluntary in the absence of a requirement to remedy the discriminatory practices disclosed by the information reported.
That is what we have here. We have procedures which will mean companies will be reporting information which could be entirely revealing of inadequacies, ongoing discrimination, and the lack of measures to deal with that. That would not cut them off at all. The report goes on:
A requirement of public reporting may result in public pressure on a company to revise its systems but it is unrealistic to rely on public opinion as an effective monitoring agent. It results in a speculative and scattered approach and creates the perception, in the absence of enforcement, that the issue is deserving of only casual attention.
Casual attention is precisely what we do not want. Studies have all too amply documented the extent of discrimination, low wages and salaries, of these target groups; the very high percentage of unemployment among disabled and native people; the concentration of women in ghettoized sectors of the economy without opportunities for job advancement. In the case of women, they have plenty of qualifications. Often they are over-qualified for the job, but there is still systemic discrimination and the measures in this Bill simply do not deal with that. The report goes on:
Voluntary programs of various kinds on behalf of women were attempted in Canada after the Royal Commission on the Status of Women reported in 1970. Certain of these programs were revitalized and expanded, at least in the public sector in and after 1975, International Women's Year. Voluntary programs in the federal government have had little impact on the composition of the public sector workforce.
It is shameful to see the low proportion of women in these jobs and, of course, the heavy concentration in the lower paying, dead-end jobs which do not lead to promotion.
Let me refer also to the observations of the Urban Alliance on Racial Relations which presented a very excellent brief on this subject. This organization deals with visible minorities and has conducted studies on the extent of discrimination that they experience, and I think it has some very wise advice for the Government. It points out that the Government has not announced requirements for departmental affirmative action plans, the goals and timetables for increasing the representation of these target groups. It does not say whether, when and in what form government Departments will report publicly on their progress or what sanctions will be imposed by Treasury
Board on Departments which do not make progress towards equality. All of this, unfortunately, is true. This legislation is seriously lacking in this area.
The initiative regarding equal pay for work of equal value is long overdue. The Government has been bound by the Canadian Human Rights Act which requires this, but there is no timetable for implementation and no indication of the amount of money set aside to equalize women's pay. This remains a vain hope, an ideal somewhere off in the sky, but there are no realistic measures and penalties for failure to comply. Treasury Board has been responsible for affirmative action in the Government of Canada for some years now and women have little to show for it. Goals set for increasing women's representation have been very low and they have only been set for management positions where women are largely excluded. Target groups have no reason to consider Treasury Board a credible agency in the affirmative action field. They have been told about what they are lacking for a long time. There has been extensive lobbying and Treasury Board has been on the other side when groups representing workers are negotiating a better situation for women. Treasury Board does not want to see classification changed. It imposes artificial limitations on opportunities for women's promotion and advancement.
The Government of Canada has announced that Crown corporations will be required to have affirmative action plans and report to Treasury Board. Some Crown corporations will be required to report publicly. However, the Government has not announced the requirements for these affirmative action plans. It has not announced goals and timetables for achieving appropriate representation of the four target groups. There are no sanctions to be applied to Crown corporations if they do not produce results.
We know how bad Crown corporations have been. 1 personally have been lobbying the CBC since 1974. Its record is abysmal in hiring and promoting women into the creative production and managerial positions. This is typical of the backwardness of our Crown corporations. Crown corporations which fall under the legislation governing federally-regulated businesses will not have to begin to report their workforce data for three years. Why should there be this kind of delay? Why should we not be moving into mandatory affirmative action promptly? They have had plenty of time. The Royal Commission on the Status of Women in Canada reported in 1970. One of the recommendations was that each Crown corporation have a plan for the implementation of the recommendations of the Royal Commission's report. For 16 years they have known that the people of Canada expect some action toward employment equity. For 16 years they have been stalling, and we now have legislation before us which would give them another three years to stall.
Contracts give the Government of Canada a major opportunity to have some impact. Billions of dollars a year are spent on Government contracts for goods and services across the country. This is a carrot which could be used to encourage
November 21, 1985

corporations doing business with the Government to clean up their acts. Instead, we have a very weak approach which includes only the major corporations, and under very weak provisions at that. This is an opportunity to involve the medium-sized and even small businesses which want Government business. For them the government contracts would be a decided incentive to clean up their acts and introduce employment equity.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I will just point out that the legislation is woefully inadequate. We cannot support it. We call on the Government to take a good, hard look at it and to do justice for women, disabled persons, native persons and visible minorities. It is about time that we had some good, hard adequate legislation with timetables, goals, and mechanisms for enforcement in order to create a situation where people have a fair chance in the workforce.

Mr. Speaker, not only do I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on Bill C-62, I feel that as a woman, and especially as the Minister for Youth, I have a duty to do so because, Mr. Speaker, it is essential to get back to a subject that is very important to us, who belong to a highly industrialized world and claim to live in a modern and progressive society.
I think everyone will readily admit that high principles and noble ideals do not readily become a living part of our culture, and that it is easy to forget the principles of justice, equality and equity, and even the idea of long term benefits.
That is why Governments must intervene to keep individual aspirations from infringeing on the rights of the community. And that is what led to the creation, in June 1983, of the Royal Commission on Equality and Employment. In October 1984, the Commission's report was submitted by the chairman of the Commission, Judge Rosalie Abella.
I shall, if I may, read a passage from the report. It is taken from Chapter 6 and concerns instruments of implementation. We read: It would also be expected that employers would set annual internal objectives but these would not be required by statute.
This recommendation from the Abella report brings us straight to the core of Bill C-62, which is now at the second reading stage. Clause 4 of the Bill establishes the employer's duty, in two respects:
To eliminate employment practices not otherwise authorized by law that result in employment barriers, and to institute policies and practices to ensure that the persons concerned achieve equitable representation.
Mr. Speaker, it is true that Bill C-62 does not provide any penalties for employers who fail to observe the letter and the intent of the legislation. Some see this as a serious shortcoming. However, those who do can hardly have spent much time reading and examining the Bill before the House today.
Employment Equity
Although the Bill does not contain any provisions that make achieving tangible and concrete results compulsory, that is not the case with the submission of reports. Indeed, Clause 6 tells us that an employer who fails to meet his obligation to produce the report prescribed in Clause 5 is liable to a fine of up to $50,000.
I do not know many companies that would want to be fined $50,000. Nor do I know any that would work very hard at submitting statistics that failed to reflect the true situation in their establishments.
So this particular provision of the Bill indicates the Government is firmly resolved to make federally-regulated businesses eliminate discriminatory employment methods and practices and substitute therefor such measures and practices that are likely to guarantee target group members that the principle of equity in recruitment, promotion and remuneration will be observed. It is this provision that will provide justice for women, native peoples, the handicapped and members of visible minorities, who have been left out of the labour market for too long. And that same provision will also provide a measure of justice for those who are being doubly discriminated against. I am referring to young women, young native people, young handicapped persons and young members of visible minorities.
People who think that getting a job right away is the sole concern of young people today do not know much about what young people are thinking nowadays. Today, they are thinking about post-secondary education, the environment, culture, and the practical job experience they can get while they are still at school. I think that as a result of these measures, they can expect to find jobs when the time comes, even if they belong to groups that usually have even more trouble finding employment.

Employment, Mr. Speaker, is not the only thing that preoccupies young people today. They want to talk about postsecondary education, the environment, the cultural aspects of life, peace, and pre-employment practical experience. Above all, Mr. Speaker, they want to talk about participation in the life of the country and the decision-making process of the country. They all want to be part of society in general. More than any others, the young women, the handicapped young people and the aboriginal young people find this difficult. It is through a Bill like C-62 that we will be able to achieve that for them.

Mr. Speaker, in our present situation, anyone who thinks that young people, and I realize I am repeating myself, see today's job as their sole concern is really oversimplifying the problem. It is with legislation like this Bill that over time, the advancement of women and all other minorities, all members of these target groups, will make enormous strides. As far as I am concerned, a vote against this Bill is a vote against the

Employment Equity
youth of this country. It is a vote against women, young native people, young handicapped persons and against all visible minorities, and I cannot imagine how anyone in this House could be against the advancement of those who in ten or fifteen years will be the leaders of this country. If we do not take them seriously today, we deserve to get the same treatment when, in a few years' time, they will be sitting where we are now.
I therefore ask all Members of this House ... I think we must, all of us together, take this important step towards equity, towards justice for young people and the other groups.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with some interest to the speech of the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne). You cannot help but feel sympathy for some of the things she expresses, concerns not only of hers but concerns of the overwhelming majority of people in the country. I listened also to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) who spoke about the need to proceed with this legislation because it was a step forward. Yet you have to stop and ask yourself, is it a step forward when you put in legislation and write into law something that you cannot enforce? Is that a step forward when you write a law that has absolutely no enforcement mechanism within it?
If we were to treat other sectors, other problems in society in the same way, we would have chaos. It is entirely possible now for companies and organizations operating in Canada to do all of the things that this Bill now requires, yet they do not. What therefore leads us to believe that as a result of having an unenforcible law companies will suddenly rush to comply with it? This is confusing to many people who view the Government's action and makes it aggravating for many of us who, for years-and I am not speaking just of opposition Members-have been arguing in some cases for what is now called employment equity but which in years gone by took on a variety of different names. We have all argued that discrimination in the workplace should cease.
When I listened to Government Members speak about a step forward, why did they not simply write a letter to everybody and tell people it is the desire of the Government that companies should do this thing and if they do, that would be nice and if they do not, do not worry about it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: It takes too long by mail.

If it does take too long by mail as the Hon. Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) says, that is the Government's problem too, is it not, Mr. Speaker? Do not foist that on us. A year and a half has gone by and there is still no action.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, what we are doing is sending out yet another signal identical to the signal sent out year after year after year. Surely to God we do not think that somehow
or other, by virtue of the passage of this piece of legislation all of those people, who until now have refused to comply with what is reasonable and fair in our society, are suddenly going to start complying.
Does the Government truly believe that those individuals who have refused to maintain in their place of work safety standards sufficient to protect their employees will voluntarily introduce employment equity? Does the Government believe that those who have traditionally relied on women and paid them low, substandard wages will certainly alter their view of life, because we think it is a good idea, and will establish without any kind of enforcement mechanism a change in the practices pursued throughout their entire business careers?
I find it incredible that Government Members would rise one after another and attempt to leave the impression that the end result of this legislation will be a change in the attitude of Canadian employers, and that, as a result of our having nodded yes, we need to have employment equity, companies will rush to institute it. If they do not, we are going to be very disappointed, are we not, Mr. Speaker? We will be very disappointed if companies do not comply, but if they do not, there is nothing we can do because there is nothing in the Bill that will allow us to take any action to require compliance with what each and every Member of this Chamber, I hope, believes is necessary in a modern society.
I want to deal primarily with the problems of women. Time does not allow me to go into details on the other areas, those of visible minorities or the natives. We all know that the report of the Special Committee on Visible Minorities in Canadian society called Equality Now set out clearly what the problems were and set out the need for action by the Parliament of Canada to require compliance with fairness and equity. But did we see a great rush of people dashing forward to implement the recommendations voluntarily? No, we did not. What did we get, Mr. Speaker? We got the Abella Report. Judge Abella in her equality and employment report says that we should require, not ask, not cajole, all federally regulated employers in both the public and the private sector to implement what she calls employment equity, which for years was called affirmative action. We have seen the groundwork laid. There were countless other reports over the last decade and beyond dealing with it. Did anyone rush forward after Judge Abella's Report was tabled and immediately begin to implement policies in the federally regulated private and public sectors voluntarily? No, Mr. Speaker.
Are we thinking that because we pass a toothless law everyone will rush forward to comply? Would you put in a speed limit without some kind of penalty for breaking it, Mr. Speaker? Of course not. Would you allow people to pollute our drinking water without some penalty for having polluted it? I should not have asked that question because the Government might in fact do so.
Oh, oh!

As I think about it now, that was not a very good analogy to draw. Let me assume goodwill if nothing else.

In this Bill we have something that goes to the very fundamental principles of society, equality for people, regardless of sex, regardless of background. We say to people at this late stage in the middle 1980s, "We are going to write a little law, if you want to live up to it, fine, and if you do not, do not worry about it because there is nothing we can do about it. We will be mad at you and if we are really mad, you will have to suffer the consequences of our annoyance." That is the extent of it and that is not good enough, Mr. Speaker. That is why we say that this is not a step forward. It may even be a step backward. It is entirely possible that by virtue of the introduction and passage of this legislation complacency will become rampant in the country, if you can imagine rampant complacency.
Oh, oh!
That tells you something about it.
Rampant complacency is not any different from progressive conservatism.
Oh, oh!

As my colleague says, rampant complacency is not any different from progressive conservatism.
When dealing with the question of women in society, why do we need to have a law with some kind of enforcement mechanism in it? We need it because the average earnings of women in the paid workforce are 60 per cent of the average earnings of men, notwithstanding the fact that for years people have said there should be equality in the pay of those doing similar kinds of work. Women workers are still confined to most of the job ghettos. Three out of five work in clerical, sales or service occupations.
I draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker, that computer technology is invading the area in which women used to work, so they are not getting a chance at those jobs. At present, 52 per cent of Canadian women work outside the house, 42 per cent of families headed by women have incomes below the poverty line, and 62 per cent of elderly women live below the poverty line. By the end of the century, women's labour force participation rate is expected to be equal to that of men.
I see you signalling, Mr. Speaker; I am just winding up. During the last 10 years, the average unemployment rate of women was 9 per cent, while it was just over 7 per cent for men.
I make these points in order to reinforce what I am trying to say. We have known of these things for years. The discrepancies and discrimination have existed for years. People have written about it. There have been reports about it. There have been requests and requirements for years. However, there has never been a law with teeth in it. Now we have yet another toothless law. I say to the Government that we are opposed to it because we frankly believe that it will set back the cause of equality in the workplace rather than enhance it.

Mr. Speaker, it is both a duty and a pleasure to rise again on a matter of considerable interest to the Conservative Party, Bill C-62 on employment equity which I unreservedly champion. 1 regret that our Canadian parliamentary system is such that, as a result of the will and directives of their Party, Members of the Opposition-and particularly my female colleagues on the other side-cannot endorse this measure. What a shame!
While I would not for a moment entertain the thought that the principles of those Members who are against the measures advocated with respect to the designated groups might in any way spring from theories which had wide currency in Europe in the 1930s, I can only conclude that the position taken by some opponents of our propositions is likely to debase our country's reputation in terms of respect for all Canadian men and women, especially those who belong to the designated groups; visible minorities, persons with disabilities, aboriginal peoples, women. Canada is made up of immigrants from every corner of the world, and a stroll along the streets of any major Canadian city will bear witness to that. People of all races, colours and cultures can be seen every day.
As to persons with disabilities, examples abound, for they are active in all circles and all spheres of society, and public transportation, access roads to buildings and city sidewalks have been designed to meet their needs. A number of companies have rolled out the welcome carpet for disabled people, a reliable source of qualified, assiduous and devoted employees.
As to aboriginal peoples, their presence in our major northern cities is ever more apparent, and companies which develop our natural resources increasingly look to them as a pool of skilled workers.
Another of the main designated groups whose sheer numbers give it preponderance-women. A lot of ground has been covered since the first women's groups took position at the turn of the century and, as a result of changing economic needs and new trends in social values, a great many women have sought to enter or re-enter the labour market.
As I have just shown, Mr. Speaker, Canada is a welcoming land, a land of warm hospitality and great diversity, a country where a foreigner wants to sink his or her roots and where peace and justice prevail. How justice has become a trite concept! Some people claim that any man or woman is entitled to possess all the wordly goods he or she can afford to buy and that we all have equal opportunities to better our own lot. Others maintain that we are all entitled to the same standard of living and that our overall wealth should be equally divided among us all.
Were we to adopt that approach we would run the risk of opening ever unresolved debates which could only prop up the cause of those who prefer to stand pat rather than forge ahead.

Employment Equity
Unlike previous Governments we have faced the facts and taken constructive measures.
Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservative Party admits that the designated groups I mentioned are victims of discrimination in employment. The Progressive Conservative Party acknowledges that, however numerous they may be in this country, members of visible minorities are denied employment equity because of the colour of their skin. We know that. The Progressive Conservative Party agrees that, despite some progress, the professional potential of the disabled is shamefully exploited and that a good many of them simply cannot claim their rightful place in the labour force.
We have acknowledged the fact that, while an increasing number of native people live and work in northern centres, they still have a disastrous unemployment rate and very little access to the labour market. We have recognized that, while women have recently seemed to be better appreciated on the labour market, their wages are still less than one third those paid to men and they are still mostly confined to so-called traditional occupations in three sectors, namely sales, services and teaching.
Mr. Speaker, this Government has recognized these facts and taken concrete action to rectify the situation. Following the recommendations of the Abella Report, this Government has introduced Bill C-62 to provide employment equity to women, the native people, the handicapped and the members of visible minorities and give them the same rights as other citizens for recruitment, promotion and salaries.
Mr. Speaker, we believe that we have proven our case. The arguments against this Bill have simply melted away. There is no basis to the suggestions that passage of this Bill will entail considerable expenses.
On the one hand, the amounts that the Government will have to spend in this regard are minimal. On the other hand, the cost to businesses will be quite reasonable and indeed insignificant when compared with the enormous benefits which will be gained by employers in acquiring an enthusiastic, assiduous, quick, faithful and competent manpower.
Mr. Speaker, I repeat that we have proven our case. The Government has recognized the facts and taken action. Parliament must do the same. It must accept the facts and pass without further delay the Bill now under consideration which will enshrine in our statutes the principle of employment equity.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I remember that, in 1976, I was working for a large company, Esso Imperial, in the comfort centre department, and after going up through the ranks, I had attained a level where I was blocking the promotion opportunities of my colleagues.
Such was the climate at the time.

One day, I was called to the director's office, where I was told: "Mrs. Bourgault, we have to transfer
you and offer you a position in Don Mills, Ontario, because you cannot be appointed to a management position." I asked why and the reply was: "Because you are a woman and the company finds it difficult to recognize that a woman could be manager of the heating system installation department." Ten years after this, we are still discussing employment equity. We are not about to forget the work of all the women who, for a hundred years, have been making every effort to attain their rightful place in this country and make people recognize that their work and education are just as good as those of their male colleagues.
When your parents pay for your university studies, Mr. Speaker, the fact that you are a woman makes no difference. The fees are the same as for a man. It costs the same.
You pay the same for your lodgings and studies. Why is it that you cannot get the same wages after joining the labour market? This is a problem which must be addressed and our Government has recognized it. Bill C-62 attempts-1 am sorry, Mr. Speaker, I would like to withdraw that word-aims at solving this problem.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with much attention to the remarks made by the Hon. Member who has just resumed her seat, and I can tell her that her promotion at Esso's, on the basis of the arguments she has put forward . . . she should not think that she was refused a promotion because of her sex.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has suggested that she feels it is unfortunate that the Parliamentary system does not allow us to vote in favour of this Bill. I understand that she is a newcomer to the House and that, being part of this Government, she has never had the opportunity to vote freely or according to her choice. I want nevertheless to inform her, Mr. Speaker, that she has the right to vote according to her conscience like all other Members of this House, and that if the Conservative Party has not told her so yet, I urge her to consult our Standing Orders.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has told us just how everything is fine and dandy in this best of all possible worlds, she has mentioned the case of the handicapped whom she sees as perfectly integrated everywhere in the labour force. Either the Hon. Member is living in a world of make-believe, Mr. Speaker, or she does not understand the reality and problems of people afflicted with a physical or mental handicap. Mr. Speaker, she mentioned the native people who were so active in the major urban centres of the North. Has she ever been to the North, Mr. Speaker? In the North, major urban centres just do not exist, Mr. Speaker. If she has visited all parts of Canada, all she has to do is to check the statistical data concerning the under-employment of native people and she will realize
November 21, 1985

that the preamble to her remark was completely wrong. Mr. Speaker, she insisted that the Progressive Conservative Party is aware of the problem. Then she said that the Progressive Conservative Party is aware of the problem experienced by the handicapped, the visible minorities, the native people, and finally Canadian women. Her conclusion: it is so very much aware of it that it has decided to push through Bill C-62. But let us try to answer one question, Mr. Speaker: Is there anything in this Bill which would have solved the problem experienced by my hon. friend at the time she was working for Esso? There is nothing, because the Esso Company would have had no obligation under this Bill. She has said that the case is closed, but I feel that the advocates were quite poor, Mr. Speaker. If the case of women, the handicapped, the visible minorities and the native people has been heard by the Government, I do not understand its decision to introduce such a weak Bill as this.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-62 is only wishful thinking on the part of the Government. You know as I do that there is nothing in this Bill to force anybody to do anything, except table a report, and not in every case, only a number of companies with contracts amounting to $200,000 or more; yet, small- and medium-sized businesses which have provided the bulk of jobs over the past ten years are automatically excluded by this $200,000 restriction. Where does the Hon. Member think she will have any influence with her worthless bill? How could she go through the mental exercise of reading the Abella Report and then feel that this was an adequate response? I am sure that if she has read the Abella Report, she must have seen that mandatory measures and a strong mechanism were required to make employment equity a reality and not just wishful thinking, Mr. Speaker. This is what was called for in the Abella Report. The report called for the establishment of a specialized agency to ensure that actual, everyday equality be implemented. Where is that agency in Bill C-62? It is nowhere to be found. This means nobody will be there to enforce those great principles which Government Members are so self-righteously bragging about.
It is a fact, Mr. Speaker, that this Bill could have been replaced by an ad in the papers. The impact would have been the same. Nothing at all has been gained with our wasting the time of the House when all we want is to urge to action, to gently tap employers on the back and tell them to go ahead. But there is nothing, no teeth in that legislation. What kind of Government is this? Have they got any backbone? If they have identified the problem, where are the solutions? Certainly not in that flaccid Bill they are putting forward. And worse still, Mr. Speaker, listen to the kind of speeches we have been hearing since this morning. They would have the people believe that starting from now, there is no longer any problem, that those groups will be considered on an equal footing. The Hon. Member will go back to her constituency and tell women: "Do not worry, we now have as many opportunities as everyone
