else". Not with that Bill, Mr. Speaker. She should go back to the drawing board and reconsider her Bill. I hope the Conservative Members will not have the gall to tell the handicaped in their constituencies that this House has passed a bill that will bring them tremendous benefits, for they will be very disappointed, because this has no real-life meaning for them.
I hope the Government Members will not lie to the natives by telling them that from now on they will have as many opportunies as everybody else to make it on the labour market. Actually, this is not the case. The Bill only contains the pious wishes of a cowardly and spineless Government.
Mr. Speaker, this Bill was analysed by Lise Bissonnette, a well-known journalist, and her conclusion is that this legislation is only symbolic. She says that it simply proposes a disguised optional program. Mr. Speaker, why does the Government take the trouble to have this Bill passed if it will then misrepresent the situation to the groups involved? 1 trust that the Hon. Member will look at her own conscience and rise freely to say: "This is not good enough." Her personal experience with Esso will show her that this Bill will do absolutely nothing for her. Since she does not want other women to suffer the same humiliation as she did, she will go to the Minister responsible and tell her: "Your Bill does not respond to the needs of real life." At least, I hope that she will do so. I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary, who has a lot more influence than any of us on the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), is listening and taking notes and that he will recommend to his Minister that some teeth be put into this Bill.
The Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne) tried to suggest that this legislation will do a lot for young people. There is as much in this for youth as she had in her Youth Year and as she will have under her own portfolio after January 1. In other words, there is absolutely nothing for young people in this Bill. I do not understand how she can have the audacity to rise today and pretend that there is.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that, after looking at this Bill, all the Members of this House and the groups concerned will be able to see that the Government is simply being wishful while its cowardice is very obvious.

Mr. Speaker, in the brief 10 minutes available to me, I would like to remind Hon. Members of the situation that faces women in the workforce or women who are trying to get into the workforce. Then I would like to take another look at this Bill, not so much from the point of view of criticizing it, because that has been done repeatedly, but I would like to put forward in a positive way the kinds of things we would like to have seen in the Bill and the kind of things we hope will still be considered.

November 21, 1985
Employment Equity
Earlier my colleague referred to some of the statistics that apply to women in the workforce. It is now almost a cliche that women earn 60 per cent of the average wages of men. We know that 42 per cent of women family heads are poor, and this figure is increasing every week. We also know that the traditional family, the one to which we refer when we speak about family allowances-the one in which the father works, the mother is at home doing the dishes and there are two lovely children-is almost a myth in society. In fact, 52 per cent of women now work outside the home as well as in the home and 66 per cent of the workforce is at this time composed of women.
We could look ahead to the year 2000 by following the trends. We would see an even greater increase in the direction of women carrying full responsibility in the workforce. By the year 2000, two out of three of the new entrants into the workforce will be women. Yet the unemployment rate for women is higher. Let us keep in mind that the figure we now have is a very conservative one because many women who would like to work do not register with the unemployment office. Over the last 10 years, the unemployment rate for women was 9 per cent and for men it was 7.6 per cent.
1 believe we can find a very startling statistic if we look at the month of September. We heard from Government Members how many new jobs were created in September. Looking at the Statistics Canada figures very closely, we see that full-time jobs went down by 24,000 and most of those were jobs which traditionally employ women. On the other hand, there were 47,000 more part-time jobs. Most of the part-time jobs were for women. Here again there is a trend of women being forced into part-time work. Do not try to tell me that this is because they choose part-time work. It is because they do not have much choice, and in fact many of the largest companies in the federal jurisdiction, and the airlines in particular, are deliberately trying to force workers, most of whom are women, into part-time contract jobs.
The situation is bad and we had hoped that this Bill would deal with fairness within the workforce for the women who are now working. We had also hoped, of course, that there would be much more emphasis on full-time job creation, not parttime job creation, for women. We had hoped that there would be jobs with equal pay for work of equal value and jobs with equal opportunity for advancement for women.
It is very important that we look at employment equity within the federal job-creation programs. We have been told by this Government and by the former Liberal Government that employment equity is implicit in the federal job-creation programs. However, only 20 per cent of the people who benefited from the old NEED program were women. Only 13 per cent of those who benefited from the old Canada Works program were women and only 38 per cent of those who benefited from the LEAP program were women. I am going to be looking very carefully at the figures for the new job-creation programs to see what happens.
Only 5 per cent of the people going into apprenticeship programs in 1981 were women. Only .5 per cent of the workers
in non-traditional jobs were women. We can see that women are still stuck in the old job ghettos consisting of jobs that are being fast affected by technological change. These jobs include clerical, sales and service jobs, three out of five of which employ women. Very few women are entering non-traditional jobs or getting training for those jobs.
Let us look at management. Affirmative action and employment equity is supposed to be targeted at getting more women and minority groups to move up the scale. They are targeted at not only getting women into the jobs and into decent-paying jobs but at giving women an opportunity to advance. Members of Parliament should be ashamed of the fact that in the Public Service on which we have a direct impact, only 6 per cent of management jobs are held by women, yet 80 per cent of those who hold administrative or clerical jobs and the like are women. This is really intolerable when for years we have been talking about affirmative action in the Public Service. It just goes to show that even though it is now called employment equity and not affirmative action, voluntary programs do not work.
Ever since I have been in the House, and that is getting on to seven years now, the Government has said that voluntary affirmative action will work. It does not even work in the public sector on which we have a direct impact and for which there are unions as well. Let us not be naive about this.
We feel that this Bill should include more provisions and we hope that the Government will seriously consider withdrawing this Bill in order to make major changes to it. If we are to have employment equity or affirmative action, whichever name we want to call it, and if it is going to work, we believe very strongly, as do the authorities in this field, that there must be one central agency that is in charge of enforcement and the establishment of standards.
In the federal jurisdiction, there are four different areas to consider: federal Departments, Crown corporations, contractors and federally-regulated businesses. These are the four areas on which we should have direct impact in imposing employment equity. As well, unions should be involved in the planning of employment equity at all stages. That is another thing that has been forgotten in this Bill.
As my colleagues have said repeatedly, if we are to have employment equity programs that will achieve true equality in the workforce, we have to have a mandatory program and not a voluntary one. We have to have a program the goals of which are clearly defined and established, and there has to be a program with timetables for achieving a greater participation of women and minorities in each job situation.
An enforcement agency must be able to receive, analyse and publicize employer' workforce data. There is a fair bit in this Bill about reporting requirements. Perhaps the Bill is not so bad from the standpoint of reporting, but if that is all we are going to require, then we should forget it. We should simply do a reasearch project.
We feel that there must be a way of imposing program requirements and penalties on employers who do not comply
November 21, 1985

with the expected established targets and timetables. There must be penalties but there are none provided for in this Bill. The Bill does provide a slight penalty for not keeping records, but nothing beyond that.
We feel that there must be a way of investigating the programs, practices and data systems of employers so that reporting is not simply left to the initiative of the employers. There also must be a real channel for complaints or court action. We do not feel it is good enough that individual workers, most of whom are women, have to go case-by-case to take a complaint to the Human Rights Commission. Every single employer in the federal jurisdiction should provide equal pay for work of equal value. This should not even be questioned and there should be no need for complaints. We should make a systemic change in that direction.
We feel that there must be contract compliance and that this is not defined clearly enough in the Bill. Contract compliance must be imposed on all Government contractors with over 50 employees and $200,000 worth of Government contracts per year. Contractors must also provide equal pay for work of equal value.

Mr. Speaker, the citizens of New Brunswick are concerned about the federal Government's intention to subsidize the reopening of the Cyprus Anvil mine in the Yukon Territory.
According to several observers, this reopening of the mine would result in a reduction of the prices of lead and zinc, making several other Canadian mines hardly profitable.
In my province, the Brunswick mine, in Bathurst, could not stand a new price reduction of its minerals. Its profit margin was considerably cut as a result of the low prices of the past few years. The reopening of the Cyprus Anvil mine would be catastrophic.
Another example is the Heath Steele mine, in Newcastle, which was closed two years ago because of a glut of zinc and lead on the market. If prices continue to go down, its chances of resuming operation are non-existent.
Mr. Speaker, I am not against the principle of creating jobs in the North, but knowing that the reopening of the Cyprus Anvil mine would result in other Canadian mines being less profitable, the Government should know that the second consequence of this reopening would be a major loss of jobs in New Brunswick and elsewhere.
How could the Government justify using federal funds to create jobs in one area, when it is aware that this decision could result in jobs being lost in another elsewhere in this country?

Mr. Speaker, Canadian Pacific Railway recently notified its pensioners of its intention to withdraw their travel privileges. Improvements to the medical plan, of little use in some provinces, were offered to the pensioners as a saw-off.
Unfortunately pensioners were never consulted on whether or not they wanted this change. Many of them have complained to me and to other Members of Parliament about this unilateral change to their retirement benefits. Pensioners feel, quite legitimately, that they are being deprived of a benefit they earned during their working lives.
Clearly, it is not satisfactory that a company make such a unilateral change. Regulations should limit companies in making retroactive changes to the benefits of retired workers. CP Rail should reconsider these insensitive changes.
 * *

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Government passed Bill C-49, an Act to amend the Criminal Code (prostitution).
Such important changes clearly show Canadians that our Government is carrying on with its job of dealing out the correctives needed by our society.
Mr. Speaker, in spite of the objections raised by the Liberals and New Democrats, the incidence of prostitution will be reduced thanks to the Conservatives.

November 21, 1985
We have seen no demonstrations organized by the Opposition on Parliament Hill like the ones they had with respect to family allowances and old age security pensions.
Mr. Speaker, when it is a matter of cleansing the morals of people, why is the Opposition not gathering our virtuous mothers or our respected older citizens together in support of the Government in its relentless task of eradicating prostitution?
When it comes to dealing with problems of moral depravation, the Opposition outcry is no longer heard.
We have been elected to bring about those changes. Mr. Speaker, as a Government we assume our responsibilities. A word to the wise is enough.

Mr. Speaker, approximately 80 farm families in my constituency of Cardigan, Prince Edward Island, grow tobacco. With declining demand for tobacco, an orderly reduction in production capacity is necessary in order to prevent damaging repercussions to growers. The P.E.I. industry supports the reduction plan and feels that each province should share proportionately in relation to its production.
In order to avoid financial disaster, and to aid growers who must find new means of earning a livelihood, financial assistance from Ottawa is necessary. Compensation to producers for loss of productive capacity must be in direct proportion to their contribution to the generation of tax dollars from production.
The Government must also establish a mechanism with producer-provinces to pay out compensation. The P.E.I. industry has proposed that each province's share of compensation be based on a five-year average of domestic production. In this way Ontario would receive 83.4 per cent; Quebec, 10.3 per cent; Prince Edward Island, 4.9 per cent; and Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, 1.5 per cent. I would urge the Government to act quickly to help all of Canada's producers through a difficult period of adjustment, in a fair and equitable manner.

subtopic: REPORTED USE OF AGENTS PROVOCATEURS BY GOVERNMENT OF INDIA
REPORTED USE OF AGENTS PROVOCATEURS BY GOVERNMENT OF INDIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last June an Air-India Jet originating in Canada crashed off the coast of Ireland with the loss of 329 lives. Since that time the entire Sikh community of Canada has been under a cloud of suspicion and innuendo with the suggestion that some of its people were responsible for the crash. Federal investigation encouraged this suspicion when police raided the Sikh Temple at Duncan, British Columbia, violating their sacred space, even though the police found nothing to take.
A story in today's Globe and Mail now claims the Government of India has been using agents provocateurs to destabilize the entire Sikh community. People posing as religious fanatics have worked to discredit all members of the Sikh faith who have advocated an independent homeland in the Punjab. These very serious charges require clarification by federal authorities.
The Sikh people have the right to be protected by the Canadian Government. We cannot stand by if, as the article claims, a legitimate religious community within Canada is being destablized and placed under a cloud of suspicion by agents of a foreign Government. If the article lacks substance, the Government should indicate so. However, if there is substance to the Globe and Mail story, Canada must protest in the strongest terms to the Government of India about this violation of Canadian rights and freedoms.

subtopic: COMMISSION'S DECISION TO SECURE EVIDENCE IN SOVIET UNION
COMMISSION'S DECISION TO SECURE EVIDENCE IN SOVIET UNION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to echo the concerns of my hon. colleagues from Calgary East, Edmonton East, and Parkdale-High Park with respect to the Deschenes Commission ruling on the advisability of travelling to the Soviet Union to take evidence. In his ruling Mr. Justice Deschenes clearly stressed that six basic precautions must be applied to the collection of Soviet evidence to counter the very real danger of abuse and subversion of the rule of law. In referring to the six precautions Mr. Justice Deschenes states that: "The Commission concurs in those conditions and will insist that they be accepted and observed. Failure to agree ought then to be considered as a refusal to co-operate with Canadian justice."
Are we to assume that if these conditions are not met by the Soviets then the Commission will not take the Soviet evidence? If this is the case, why not have this agreement committed to writing beforehand? I believe the six safeguards proposed by Mr. Justice Deschenes are significant and necessary, but I do not think they go far enough. For example, there should be a forensic examination of all documents to determine their validity, and this examination should take place in a neutral environment.
Consideration should only be given to evidence if it is of a corroborative nature. As well, the Commission should at least request that witness depositions be taken in Canada or at the Canadian Embassy. Without an extension of these safeguards and an agreement in writing with the Soviets, 1 cannot support the Commission's decision to travel to the Soviet Union to take evidence.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR MAINTENANCE OF FOOTWEAR AND TEXTILE
REQUEST FOR MAINTENANCE OF FOOTWEAR AND TEXTILE
speechtext:
Again yesterday, Mr. Speaker, we saw the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) break his word. And again, that promise had been made in Sherbrooke during the election campaign. We all remember the Prime Minister's famous promise to the elderly in Sherbrooke, a promise which he was forced to swallow.
And then in the month of May, in Sherbrooke, in the Eastern Townships, he had promised to maintain footwear and textile quotas, but again yesterday the Prime Minister did not keep his word and footwear quotas went by the board.
Mr. Speaker, this inhuman Government is unable to tell us . .. Today's headline in the Journal de Montreal reads: "5,000 Quebec shoe workers will lose their jobs". The Government is unable to tell us where these workers will find other jobs.
Montreal East is already threatened with the loss of 5,000 jobs because of the inaction of this Government. Two groups of people from Daoust and La Parisette in Montreal East came here to see if anything could be done to help them, but what they heard yesterday was the end of it and, without quotas, other shoe factories will have to shut down as a result of this Government's stupid and inhuman decisions.
Mr. Speaker, I dare hope that the 58 Quebec Conservative Members-described as cowards yesterday by the union president-will wake up and convince the Prime Minister that he has to honour his commitments and maintain quotas.

Mr. Speaker, on November 1, 1985, rail passes for all CP Rail pensioners in Canada were revoked and replaced by an extended health care package. This action by CP Rail was taken unilaterally without consultation with the pensioners. The extended health care plan does not necessarily enhance health benefits for the

November 21, 1985

pensioners as they were already covered free of charge by provincial health plans. To the pensioners the passes were construed as a right in recognition of past employment, a right pensioners enjoyed since the inception of the railway some one hundred years ago.
It is morally wrong for CP Rail to have taken such action unilaterally against a group which has no bargaining units to defend itself. I believe such action to be questionable legally as well. Understandably, Mr. Speaker, the pensioners are upset. On their behalf I strongly urge the support of all my colleagues on both sides of the House in speaking out in order to allow CP Rail pensioners the option of retaining their pass privileges so abruptly revoked by CP Rail.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Miss MacDonald that Bill C-62, an Act respecting employment

November 21, 1985
Employment Equity
equity, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee, and on the amendment of Mr. Keeper (p. 8197).

Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity to speak first on this Bill before the motion to hoist was moved. Rather than reiterate some of the things I said the other day, I would like to draw the attention of the House to exactly what it is in Bill C-62 that the Liberal Opposition is opposed to with regard to the proposals made by the Government. More important, I would like to draw to the attention of the Members of the House the reasons we had the Abella Commission in the first place, the working conditions that led to the need for that kind of commission, and the exact recommendations made by Judge Abella in her report. By doing so, I will point out the inadequacies of the Government's response through Bill C-62 which is presently before the House.
The mandate of the commission, Mr. Speaker, was, in essence, the following: The Judge was asked to inquire into the most efficient, effective and equitable means of promoting employment opportunities for, and eliminating systemic discrimination against, four designated groups: women, native people, disabled persons, and visible minorities. In the 11 Crown and Government-owned corporations, the improvement rate for women over the five-year period studied had been minimal. Women remained overwhelmingly concentrated in the lowest paid occupations in every corporation. In fact, the Judge found that they held very few managerial or supervisory positions.
As a result of the first study that was done, the Liberal Government in power at the time undertook a pilot project at the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which is singled out as an example of success in elimination of discriminatory barriers in employment. It was found that only in those corporations where measures have been implemented to eliminate discriminatory barriers in employment have opportunities for women genuinely improved. All corporations agreed that without legislation and a reporting requirement substantial change was unlikely to occur. Bear that in mind, Mr. Speaker, because that is a very important element in the reasons for the Liberal Party's opposition to Bill C-62 in its present form.
When Judge Abella went across the country gathering evidence most representatives with whom she met considered further Government intervention necessary to ensure their equitable participation in the workforce. The report also concluded that it is critical that census data relating to the quality of labour force participation of the four designated groups be collected every five years. Judge Abella found that employment barriers articulated by the group included insufficient or inappropriate training facilities, inadequate information systems, inadequate hiring and promotion practices and discriminatory assumptions.
The Abella Commission concluded that voluntary measures are an unsatisfactory response to the pervasiveness of systemic discrimination in Canadian workplaces and have, therefore, recommended that all federally regulated employers be
required, by legislation, to implement employment equity. In other words, it decided that there had to be a mandatory affirmative action program instituted, and several ways were recommended in which to oversee and ensure that the intent of the legislation is sound.
The first recommendation to ensure that this kind of discrimination was being eliminated was to expand the jurisdiction of the Canadian Human Rights Commission to make it responsible for employment equity. You will note, Mr. Speaker, that that is one of the recommendations in Bill C-62. It is unusual, though, that in diluting that proposal of the Abella Commission the Government has indicated that the Canadian Human Rights Commission will be the regulatory body that is going to oversee the implementation of these proposals but, in fact, it has not mandated additional resources to the Canadian Human Rights Commission through this Bill, nor has it given that body jurisdiction. Therefore, in terms of the enforcement provisions, we have serious reservations about the ability of the Canadian Human Rights Commission to undertake the necessary review and ensure that the four target groups are going to be allowed the employment opportunities that we know do not now exist within the federal Government or our Crown corporations. More important, they do not exist within companies with which the federal Government has contracts and does business.
This leads me to my second point, Mr. Speaker. What laws presently exist and in what ways can we improve the track record of the federal Government with respect to enhancement of employment equity? In 1977 the Canadian Human Rights Act was passed forbidding discrimination on the basis of sex. Since 1978 there have been affirmative action programs in federal Departments. I mentioned the pilot projects within CMHC. We later had the Katie Cooke Task Force Report on child care established under the Liberal administration which is presently in the possession of the Minister responsible for the Status of Women (Mr. McLean) awaiting follow-up.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That has not been reported.

The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) indicates that that is not yet reported, so it is still at report stage.
The following are the major points of criticism that the Liberal Party has with Bill C-62: First, it does not implement several of Judge Abella's key recommendations. The Bill includes no mandatory enforcement of employment equity. That, Mr. Speaker, is a very serious flaw. As outlined earlier, every group that came before the Abella Commission indicated that they felt that without mandatory enforcement there would be little progress made. They have cited case after case from the 1970s and early 1980s to reinforce that view.
Second, in this Bill there is no provision for a separate monitoring agency. As I indicated earlier, the responsibility has been conferred upon the Canadian Human Rights Commission but there have been no additional manpower resources allocated to that group. Due to the backlog of cases before the Human Rights Commission, the groups that have criticized
November 21, 1985

Bill C-62 are probably correct in their assumption that with a monitored three-year reporting program it will be the year 2000 and beyond before we get the first test case of the Abella Commission's Report before that body.
Third, without the allocation of additional resources, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Human Rights Commission will not have the power to enforce employment equity. That again flies in the face of all the evidence that was gathered by the Abella Commission over the several years during which she studied the problems of the four groups about which I spoke. In addition to the fact that we are not even going to have mandatory enforcement-we are going to have voluntary reporting-there have not been any targets set by the Government as to what each Department and companies that represent 200 employees or more must agree to in order to abide by the rules set by the Government.
As I have indicated about that reporting procedure, there has been no standardization established in Bill C-62. If there is no standardization, Mr. Speaker, then we will have three years of monitoring before anything can be put before the Canadian Human Rights Commission. We are talking, in effect, about another generation of Canadians who will have to await another Government, I suppose another Government with more of a commitment to the enhancement of employment equity than has been exhibited by the Conservative Government.
In the election campaign in the summer of 1984 the Government made a number of promises to women in particular with respect to recommendations that would flow from the Abella Commission report. This is another example of more broken promises.
Earlier today during Question Period quotes were given by my colleagues from the Province of Quebec and southwestern Ontario. These were verbatim promises made by the Conservative leader a year ago during the campaign about how he was going to ensure the viability of the Canadian shoe manufacturing industry. He broke that promise. The Government has broken promises with respect to making sure that deficit reduction would never be done at the expense of low-and middle-income Canadians. That promise was broken within 10 weeks of the Conservatives assuming office.
Here again, with the Abella Commission report, and the manner in which the Government has chosen to reply to those excellent recommendations, we have another series of broken promises and another generation that we will have to wait before we have some improvement in employment equity.
Last but not least, in addition to all the flaws I have outlined about this Bill previously, there are no penalties in the Bill for companies not complying with it. Why do we not simply tell Canadians and those four groups, the women, the native people, the disabled and the visible minorities, that Bill C-62 will not address their concerns, that it will not, in a reasonable period of time, add to their quality of life. They should be told that the Government is not prepared to move to create the
Employment Equity
kind of legislation required. Quite frankly, Bill C-62 is a sham. Those groups know it, opposition Members know it, and I would be delighted to hear perhaps a Government back-bench MP try to defend the recommendations in the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, we have before us today another instance of the degree to which the Government has adopted half measures and token efforts in replacement as a substitute for responsible, serious and enforcible legislation. I think it raises real questions about the self respect of the Government and the degree to which-
It has none.

-the Government takes its promises and preelection commitments seriously when we compare the legislation before us today with the sort of promises made before the election and the statements after the election of September 4, 1984.
I will not be repetitious, Mr. Speaker, by quoting to the Government the promises it made. I think that has been done adequately. This Bill highlights the difference to me between the sort of society which the Government would like to see us aim for and the society that I and my Party would like to see us aim for. It also highlights to a degree the difference between the sort of society that we have today and the sort of society that any of us might want to have. Notwithstanding our material prosperity in many parts of the country, though certainly not all, and the strides and gains made concerning the employment and the status of women, the minorities and the handicapped, our society is falling far short of what I would like to see.
We have to look at the state of a society in which women, as an example, receive only five-eighths of the average male's wage, in which native people suffer from greatly elevated levels of unemployment compared to the average in our society. We have to look at a society in which the job is of central and paramount importance to the individual, to the determination of his or her identity and self and how a person perceives himself or herself and his or her relationship to society. What I see are large numbers of people within society who are disadvantaged by the status quo, that status quo which this legislation does so little to change and so much to maintain.
I see people, Mr. Speaker, whose parents and grandparents suffered from unemployment. I see women who have been and are still being held back by prejudice and a failure to understand their potential, a failure to appreciate their commitment of what they are capable of doing. I see very little in this Bill that will do anything to correct those situations and move us toward a society where people will be able to compete on an equal, full basis, regarding only their talent, their ability, their skills and their commitment, and which will set aside extraneous factors such as race and sex.
The way in which the Bill is being handled in the House shows that what once were vices are now merely habits. The Government is introducing closure for the fifth time. The Government is trying to push through this inadequate little

November 21, 1985
Employment Equity
piece of legislation, as modest in its size as it is in its quality, as small in its thickness as it is in its ambition to do anything about the state of employment in our society.
I hear the Government taking the view that one cannot introduce mandatory programs for this sort of thing. We cannot push too hard. We cannot take steps that will upset anybody in the corporate environment. This reflects not only a lack of imagination and a lack of intelligence in design of an employment equity program, but it also essentially reflects a lack of adequate commitment to such programs.
Simply because we have bad examples of similar types of programs in the recent history, such as the language and the police issues in the Province of Quebec, does not excuse the federal Government from trying to produce something better, something that will better serve Canadians as we try to work toward a future of equality, a future based upon a concept, a realization and a concretization of employment equity.
I regret when we look at this legislation that there is no provision for the involvement of a union in the development of a corporate plan. I believe that many unions have pioneered the concept of employment equity and pioneered the implementation of employment equity measures in the workplace.
I recall the example of the Ontario Federation of Labour, which has been working on employment equity for women. It had a co-ordinator who was working on employment equity for people of minorities that previously had suffered a lack of equity in their employment prospects.
I believe that this has endowed our labour bodies with experience which could be put very well to use in the design of a corporate plan such as the legislation rather inadequately stipulates and rather inadequately outlines and requires.
Many others have said-and I must reiterate it-that this legislation lacks goals. It lacks guidelines for affirmative action. It lacks an effective enforcement mechanism and really effective sanctions. After all, the penalties for non-compliance are not framed to include any effect on the business which the offending company does with the Government.
I was surprised to hear the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne) say this morning that the Bill introduces employment equity. It manifestly does not, because of the restrictions in the Bill which apply to a very narrow segment of the total economy. After all, there is nothing in it about the Government itself and its commitment to employment equity. It merely, as we see it, applies to those employers who employ 100 or more employees on or in connection with a federal work undertaking. There is nothing relating to the over-all size of the enterprise. There is only a very loose definition of people connected with or employed on a federal work undertaking or enterprise.
A comprehensive affirmative action program would include contract compliance and sanctions. It would include equal pay for work of equal value. It would include some stipulations as to the provision of the faciliative mechanisms to institute
employment equity, such as education, training and child care. These things are not addressed by the Bill.
We know that with the majority which the Government has, the Bill will go through. We also know that five years or ten years from today, when the history of this sad piece of legislation is reviewed, all that could be said is that it had a marginal impact upon the introduction of employment equity in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am also very happy to join those who have already had the opportunity to speak about Bill C-62. In my humble opinion, this Bill is another exercise which shows the true nature of this Government. Bill C-62 deals with a very important issue which was of special concern during the last election and still is for the coming provincial election. We are always meeting people who draw our attention to unacceptable situations, especially as concerns the problems faced by women, in certain cases to get a job, and in other cases to get promotions. There are a great many instances of such problems and we are all aware of them. All that this Bill does is stated in clause 1, namely: 1.
1. This Act may be cited as the Employment Equity Act.
In my humble opinion, Mr. Speaker, about the only good thing that we find in this Bill is its title and its intent to recognize a fact which has existed for quite some time. However, there is obviously no real intent, no courage, no determination to attack the real problems directly.
The Bill states that recommendations will be made very nicely to some companies, and I emphasize the word "some", not necessarily in the short term, as the date mentioned is 1988, asking them to file a report and state their plans and intentions. However, Mr. Speaker, everyone recognizes that jobs are generally created by smaller businesses. These businesses, which are major producers of jobs, especially in a constituency such as mine, rarely employ more than 100 people.
Generally, when we speak about small businesses, we mean those whose work force varies between 2 and 50 employees. Everyone agrees that, when a business has over 50 employees, it becomes a company, since the very great majority of small businesses have fewer than 50. Yet, this legislation does not deal with such businesses in any way. It deals only with companies with over 100 employees. I find this measure rather timid, and for my part, it is quite enough to convince me to vote against this Bill.
On the subject of discrimination I think we all agree. We all recognize that there is a lot to do. Suffice it to know that 36 per cent of complaints filed with the Canadian Human Rights Commission, since its inception in 1976, relate to sex discrimination. Filed in 80 per cent of cases by women, those 2,300 complaints dealt especially with employment, but also with housing, recreation and credit. In my view, statistics such as
November 21, 1985

these clearly point to a situation that is so prevalent that, unfortunately, we have somewhat become used to living with such an unacceptable fact of life.
And faced with such a crying situation, all the Government finds as an answer and a response is the tabling of what it calls Bill C-62, a rehashing of pious wishes, of decidedly unrealistic expectancies, with the hope that someone else will help better the situation, that the private sector will take action, and that despite the absence of any sanctions, we can and will rely on good faith alone. But I would be most surprised if three, four, five or six years down the road, we found the slightest betterment, the slightest improvement in the situation as it now stands. Except that when the Bill comes into force, Government Members will have an opportunity to slap their own backs, to go bragging all across the country that they as a Government have solved the problem, that in spite of the Opposition's objections, legislation was passed and from now on we will be referring to professional equity. I agree that as a theme, or balloon, it is quite interesting.
However, when we consider the subject matter of the Bill, I think that it simply is ridiculing those for whom they have been working for years to improve conditions and eliminate those discriminations. The Government is practically laughing at them by introducing a Bill that solves so few problems and which finally is a statement of intent rather than a solution to concerns.
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, we had the opportunity to see how much indifference there is to that problem. Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to join in this extended debate on Bill C-62. The extra time we are giving to these deliberations reflects, to me, the importance of the topic to all Canadians.
The employment equity legislation will have a dramatic impact on the Canadian labour force-not dramatic in the sense of crisis or antagonism between special interests but, rather, dramatic in that for the first time Canadians long denied opportunities to participate fully in the economy will be able to contribute all of their skills and talents. These are not idle promises. In anticipation of this legislation businesses large and small are already calling Government offices to learn how they can apply employment equity principles to their operations. Believe me, this is good news to the millions of Canadian women, native people, members of visible minorities and disabled individuals. Something positive is happening at last. Individuals covered by the legislation are being given a chance to compete as equals.
The purpose of Bill C-62 is to provide for employment equity, that is, to guarantee everyone equal rights with respect to employment, advancement and remuneration. The legislation will require employers to implement employment equity and to demonstrate their progress by reporting annually on the results. What is wrong with that? To abide by the Bill's intent, as recommended by Judge Abella, objectives have to be set by and for each employer concerned. These objectives cannot be universal. We must consider the specific circumstances under which each business operates. The distinction between purpose and objective is very important. Matters cannot be taken in isolation. We must consider the general availability of qualified workers. Then, we need to take into account the availability of such workers within the designated groups. Finally, we need to look at whether workers are in the right location for the job.
For example, it is beyond dispute that there is an inexcusable lack of women in the engineering profession. We would like to see businesses hire more women engineers. However, when women represent only 6 per cent of all professional engineers, it would be folly to set quotas for individual businesses requiring them to hire women engineers in direct relation to the number of women in the general labour force.
I believe the Government is taking a far wiser approach. It is acknowledging individual needs and circumstances rather than setting arbitrary rules and procedures which would place both the private and public sectors into a straight jacket. It is
Employment Equity
like pointing a gun to a person's head. Yet, members of target groups need not worry that the lack of quotas can be used as an excuse for inaction. When employers covered by the legislation begin filing their mandatory reports in just a little more than two years, they will have to show that they are making constructive changes.
The data reports will enable the Canadian Human Rights Commission to play a key role in the enforcement of employment equity. Investigators from the Human Rights Commission will be able to use the reports as grounds to initiate investigations and then cover possible violations of human rights legislation. No longer will they be forced to wait for individuals or groups to file complaints. The Government has already committed itself to ensuring that the Human Rights Commission has the necessary resources to fulfil its mandate in support of employment equity.
These are major changes. Thus, it is only fair that the Government allows the private sector some time to get the systems in place and, ideally, take positive measures even before employers file their first reports. Yet, the changes will not be costly, which is an important aspect. Data from the United States shows that the reporting costs will probably amount to a little more than $1.50 per worker, a small price to pay to release the blocked talents of so many capable Canadians.
I am glad that many businesses are already discovering the advantages of employment equity. I agree that few enterprises paid heed when things were totally voluntary. However, we are now receiving some genuine interest well in advance of the implementation of this legislation.
I would ask Hon. Members to consider the case of the Westin Bayshore Hotel in Vancouver which has worked with the CEIC consultants. This business employs about 500 people. It took two people only one week to collect and analyse the data of the firm's workforce. The managers there say it takes only a small amount of their time to operate the employment equity program now that it is in place. That is a good sign. Executives at the hotel, and at other enterprises, are saying that they are pleased and surprised at how easy it is to make employment equity work. They are discovering the simple truth that equity actually helps to enhance productivity and profitability.
Bill C-62 requires that the affected companies implement employment equity and report annually on their workforce's composition. Similarly, associations and representatives of target groups covered by the legislation have a responsibility to work with their members to encourage them to acquire the necessary qualifications. I agree that this task is immense. There will be times of frustration, especially in making progress in the professions where it takes a substantial investment of time and effort to obtain the required skills. In this regard, the Government is ready to help out through programs in the new Canadian job strategy. There is support for training and skills development and projects, and proposals which take employment equity into account are going to receive priority attention.

I have been listening to Hon. Members of the opposition say they wish enforcement. That reminds me of what happens in a communistic state where everyone works. Everyone will work digging ditches, men, women, disadvantaged and all. However, we cannot enforce everything immediately. There is a great diversity of peoples and of employment opportunities.
Let me conclude with a simple but important observation. No Government can, or should, regulate every small element of economic activity. Our responsibility in this House is to provide a framework through which the economy can be as productive as possible, in an environment of social justice and fairness. Bill C-62 meets the high standards so essential to democracy. The legislation calls for real change and facilitates enforcement of human rights legislation against those who would try to defy the law's intent, but the most important and significant responsibilities must continue to rest with individuals and groups within our industries and communities. It is these Canadians; workers, employers and members of target groups, who will ensure the success of the employment equity objectives. We have a big challenge ahead, one of genuine opportunity for growth and change. I am confident that Bill C-62 is a major step in the direction of justice and equal opportunity for all and I urge other Hon. Members in this Chamber to join me in supporting its passage into law.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   AGRICULTURE SUGGESTED STUDY OF TOBACCO GROWING INDUSTRY
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   AGRICULTURE SUGGESTED STUDY OF TOBACCO GROWING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
That the Standing Committee on Agriculture be empowered to study the current state of the tobacco growing industry in Canada, taking into account various Financial and non-Financial government-assisted options available for a rationalization of the tobacco sector of agriculture which might provide appropriate solutions for all interests involved.
He said: Mr. Speaker, today I want to talk to my colleagues regarding the problems of the tobacco industry. I am asking in my motion that we refer the issue to the Standing Committee on Agriculture for its consideration.
Let me say a few words about the history of the tobacco industry in Canada and explain some of the changes that have taken place in that industry and society in general. I will then conclude with some suggestions as to initiatives which might be considered by the Standing Committee on Agriculture in an effort to relieve some of the pressures we are seeing not only on the producers of tobacco but on the surrounding communities.
This question must be considered carefully from the point of view of the communities surrounding those parts of the country where tobacco is grown. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Cardigan (Mr. Binns), rose under Standing Order 22 this afternoon and offered some very valid comments. He said that an orderly reduction in production capacity is necessary in Canada in order to prevent damaging repercussions to growers.
I support what he said on behalf of his farmers in Cardigan. I want to add that not only are we concerned about the growers, but also about the communities that surround these growers. I believe I am not only speaking on behalf of my constituents in Oxford but also for those in the riding of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), the riding of Elgin, and the riding of Haldimand-Norfolk, all of which are adjacent ridings. To a lesser degree, we have the same problem in a small area of Quebec, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
Most Members will know that the history of tobacco growing began roughly 50 years ago when it became a significant industry, particularly in the area surrounding Tillsonburg, Delhi, Aylmer and Simcoe. Prior to that the area was largely sand and was useless for agriculture of any kind. When it was found that tobacco grew very well in this area, tobacco growers flourished as well as the surrounding communities.
Once the surrounding communities began to flourish, various support service industries began to develop in those various communities. As a result, for a number of years there has been a very vibrant and excellent economy in those areas surrounding the tobacco growers.

November 21, 1985
Tobacco Growing Industry
Efowever, some changes have taken place which have threatened that economy. Let me refer to those briefly. Once that economic base was developed around the tobacco growers, a certain social fabric also developed as part of the community in which they work and live. The social situation in Canada has undergone some changes. In the last 10 years, we have noticed a decrease in the use of the product tobacco for smoking. In more recent years in both the United States and Canada, there has been a decline in the use of tobacco of about 2 per cent. I as a physician who believes that tobacco is harmful, as do by far the majority of people who are familiar with the health aspects of the use of tobacco, have to agree that the decline is desirable. I do not bemoan that decline but I do bemoan the fact that it is having a deleterious effect not only on the growers who deserve better treatment than that which they are receiving now but also on their communities. As soon as the growers begin to earn inadequate incomes, those who supply the growers and offer support services in the community begin to suffer.
If I may, I would like to read from one of the four western Ontario journals, the Western Ontario Business News. On page 1 of the September 23 edition, there appears the following:
It has required new marketing approaches and lent a sense of urgency to the search for new industries in communities like this town (Tillsonburg) of 10,000-
Tillsonburg happens to be in my riding but similar towns like Aylmer, Delhi, and Simcoe are all in somewhat desperate straits because of the rapid decline in the use of tobacco and the impact of that on all aspects of society in those communities. It is mainly because of that that I believe we should be addressing this problem in Parliament in an effort to help not only the producers make a transition into some other more useful type of agricultural pursuit but also to protect those people who have nothing directly to do with tobacco at all but are suffering extensively as a result of the severe drought.
I have already alluded to the health aspects of tobacco smoking. We do know, for instance, that the actual number of cigarettes smoked has gone from 69 billion in 1983 to just under 68 billion. It is a drop of roughly 2 per cent per year, as I already indicated.
From an economic point of view, the growers have also suffered because of the fact that our inflation rate, our cost of production and our lack of efficiency in many industries has led the price of tobacco on the foreign markets to be way out of line with the price of tobacco from other countries. We find that Latin American countries and some African countries are now able to produce tobacco at just a fraction of the cost for which we in Canada can produce tobacco. As a result of that, what were hitherto foreign markets that we could enjoy are now pretty well gone due to the price differential. Not only is there a health care factor and the costs related to the health problems caused by tobacco but there is also the economic factor of the decrease in foreign markets hitting tobacco growers all at the same time.
These two factors have come together on top of a history which has allowed for a very active economic growth in the communities affected for a number of years. Suddenly this growth is coming to an end. I would indicate to the House how one of the leading business people in Tillsonburg feels about this issue. Mr. Eugene Heath, owner of the Heath Department Store and also Vice President of the local Chamber of Commerce, had this brief word to say:
Tobacco has been instrumental in establishing Tillsonburg.
For that reason, I think it is incumbent upon us to take a look at this problem and see what we as a Parliament can do to obviate some of the hardships that are beginning to show already on the growers and those who are living in the communities affected.
I can cite, for example, the fact that a supplier to the tobacco industry, DeCloet Limited, which produces farm machinery for the tobacco industry, has laid off 79 of 140 workers in the last couple of years. We can see the effect this is having. The general impact on the growers themselves amounts to the fact that heretofore there were about 1,700 growers in the area but there are now only about 1,000 growers. This has occurred since 1976 because of the depression that has been suffered in the growing and particularly the sales of tobacco.
It is interesting to note what has happened to the manufacturing industry. Naturally, it surrounds to a large extent the area in which tobacco is produced. In 1985, the manufacturers indicated that they needed only 170 million pounds of tobacco compared to the 235 million pounds required the year before. No agreement was reached with the manufacturers so instead of having 170 million pounds being guaranteed by the manufacturers, they have now come up with an offer of only 135 million pounds guaranteed for this year. We can see that the growers are in quite a significant bind.
Let me go on to the next area which I believe is the important one. As a country generally composed of citizens who are compassionate toward each other, what can we do to assist these people in making a transition from growing tobacco, an industry which has been cut down to approximately half of what it was, to growing something else that is productive and will allow them to lead a normal life while at the same time not cause the communities to deteriorate in other ways? We can look at a number of initiatives that could be considered by the Standing Committee if and when this motion were to be referred to it.
I must say that one of the prime concerns of the growers is the establishment of a national marketing agency for tobacco. There have been a lot of misconceptions about this agency. I have received letters and I know the Minister has received many letters indicating to us that many people feel that this agency is designed to increase the selling of tobacco in the domestic market. If that is a significant point in favour of the national agency, it is not a big one at all and is perhaps one of the smallest.
The real reason to have a national agency is to give the growers a chance to combine together to maintain a price for
November 21, 1985

their tobacco that will allow them a reasonable return on their investment. The second reason for trying to establish a national agency is the fact that it will provide an opportunity to help prevent imports into Canada of tobacco leaf from those countries which can easily undersell the producers here in Canada. Some people argue that it can also be useful for export trade but with the price of our tobacco at the present time, 1 doubt that we will see much of an increase in exports of our tobacco.
Previously this year, the House saw fit to pass the legislation necessary to have the National Farm Products Marketing Board hold hearings that would allow the agency to be formed. Unfortunately, those hearings have been completed but before the report could be transmitted to the Minister, it was stopped because of an injunction through the courts brought forward by the manufacturers' council. Of course, this is disastrous to the producers for this year because they are not going to be in a position to be able to market their product. I would hope that that is one of the initiatives that we recognize as being very important for the growers. This national marketing agency will help those who are still in the business maintain a level of return on their investment that is consistent with a normal way of life.
There are other important reasons why this motion should go to the committee for consideration. I think particularly of the concept of alternate crop development. There is no doubt that there is a capacity for alternate crops in the sandy soil that exists in that part of Ontario and other parts of the country. I have heard representations from Gary Balthus of Haldimand-Norfolk and from George Demeyere, a former Chairman of the Ontario Flue-Cured Tobacco Growers' Marketing Board. These people have shown a lot of initiative over the last couple of years in developing a plan that would see tomatoes to be used for tomato paste grown in this part of Ontario. They have now interested close to 30 farmers in this project. They have developed a real protocol for the development of this plant. It is interesting to note that Canada utilizes about 110 million pounds of tomato paste per year, yet we import 80 million pounds. The time is here to seriously consider the wisdom of trying to develop tomatoes to be used in the production of tomato paste as an alternate crop. We are told that the same plant which could be used for tomato paste at one time of the year could be used, with a few alterations, for the processing of additional crops such as strawberries to the tune of about $26 million per year. Of course, there will be some spin-offs if alternate crops can be developed for the area. There will be spin-offs in terms of machinery production, employment for the area and plant nursery operations.
The people who have proposed the Southern Ontario Tomato Co-operative Incorporated have offered to provide 1.5 per cent of their profits to the Delhi Research Station, a neighbouring federal research station, to work on these alternate crops. That bodes well for the attitude of the people in the area who are trying to help themselves out of a difficult problem.
Tobacco Growing Industry
We have heard talk in the past which has given rise to some misconceptions about the $90 million of advance payments which was recently granted by the Minister of Agriculture. This was a big help to the producers this year who have been unable as of yet to sell their crops. The conception around the country is that this was a $90 million gift to the tobacco growers. It was not that at all. It was simply a repayable loan. The producers are hoping to be able to sell their crops in order to be able to repay the loans.
Another interesting area which should be looked at in committee is with respect to help which can be given to the remaining tobacco industry in terms of our tax laws. Taxes on tobacco products both federally and provincially have been increasing at a rather rapid rate so that they far exceed taxes on most other products. I argue that is somewhat unfair since it is a regressive type of tax. People who smoke are penalized the most and they are the ones who can least afford it. I think it is regrettable that we have to see these taxes increase at the rate which they have.
In the United States there has been a move to allocate one cent of tax per package of tobacco to encourage growers to go into other industries. It is an attempt to help those in the tobacco industry out of this predicament. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) should consider taking a certain amount of the large amount of tax revenue raised from tobacco products and allocate it to those growers who wish to become involved in the transition to another type of agricultural product. Not only would this be helpful in terms of encouraging growers to become involved in another type of industry, but it would be useful to the communities which surround these same industries.
I wish to make a few comments with respect to research and development which I think the Standing Committee on Agriculture might want to consider. There is need for a longterm study to be done with respect to what will happen to the tobacco industry over the next 10 years. It is estimated that although there are now 1,600 or 1,700 tobacco-growing farmers in Canada, in 10 years that number will most likely be reduced to approximately 800. These people have to be taken into account in society. We should be looking at ways and means to help them make adjustments.
The Delhi Research Station is situated in the sandy soil of Norfolk County. It has been performing research studies on tobacco and other products which can be grown in the area. We have been told by officials at the station that they are presently underfunded with respect to assistance which they could provide to tobacco growers who wish to diversify. They say that as little as $40,000 or $50,000 more would make a big difference in their program in order to increase their progress. They also acknowledge that what they call the new crop program is definitely underfunded.
Another area in terms of research which we should be pursuing and which has taken place in Carolina concerns the young green tobacco leaf which is one of the best known sources of a complete protein in the world. I am told it is a little expensive to extract the protein and make it ready for

November 21, 1985
Tobacco Growing Industry
human consumption. Of course, what is needed in this respect is more research. I am told that there will probably be some resistance from other sectors of the economy with respect to spending money on this research. I refer to the soybean producers and perhaps others. If we know that the tobacco leaf is one of the best sources of protein I think it is deplorable that this matter not be pursued in a world which is going as hungry as the world in which we live. I suggest this is an area into which the committee should look. Perhaps it should encourage our Minister of Agriculture to allocate some funds to this research.
Finally, I would like to deal with another area of research which is being conducted at the Delhi Research Station. Research is being done with respect to the need to cut back on the tars which are present in tobacco which is still being grown. Research being conducted there may well reduce some of the hazards which exist in terms of the carcinogens found in tobacco smoke.
I would like to conclude by saying that in various provinces there were at one time flourishing industries with strong supporting communities which are now suffering badly. I think the compassionate nature of Canadians tells us that they would like to see these people helped into a more productive and acceptable form of work. I encourage Members of the House to agree to refer this matter to the Standing Committee on Agriculture so that it can be given in-depth consideration. In this way we may be of some assistance to one sector of the community which is suffering very seriously.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   AGRICULTURE SUGGESTED STUDY OF TOBACCO GROWING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to support my colleague in what he has just said concerning this motion, and I cannot help remembering that Canadians not too long ago had the opportunity to learn about a somewhat contradictory situation.
The Government invested substantial amounts of money to support a campaign against the use of tobacco. It made a big fuss about the need for Canadian men and women to become aware of the dangers of tobacco, with the hope of seeing them reduced their smoking. At the same time, the Government was spending tens of millions of dollars to help tobacco growers.
I suppose that a great many Canadians have reacted the way I did and felt that these two initiatives were somewhat contradictory.
I think, however, that the motion moved by the Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) deserves our support, especially when we realize the importance of this industry for Canada.
Our hon. friends opposite are blaming us, saying we are against everything for the sake of being against everything. Well, Mr. Speaker, when legislation makes sense and is relevant, as that introduced by my hon. friend certainly is, I think that my Party makes a point to support it and encourage it. I believe this initiative deserves all our encouragement and all
our support if we stop for a few moments to appreciate the importance of the undertaking.
I was somewhat amazed to realize how many constituencies actually produce tobacco. Those constituencies are to be found in Ontario, Quebec, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. Those tobacco producing areas are in a relatively bad position to meet the changing demand for tobacco.
However, there are still many people directly involved in that industry, which for instance in the first half of 1985 was valued at $137 million, 69 per cent of which was in Ontario and 19 per cent in Quebec. And to go on with the information I have here before me, tobacco production was stable in 1985. All areas except Quebec experienced a decrease in the value of their tobacco production. More than 10,000 Canadians, Mr. Speaker, are permanently employed in tobacco production, and 40,000 other Canadians are provided with seasonal employment. And there are more than 7,000 people working in the processing of tobacco which is being done in approximately ten plants, both in Quebec and in Ontario. In 1983, 9 plants, 6 in Quebec and 3 in Ontario, produced a total of 63 billion cigarettes, which probably was much too high.
We are facing a situation that is quite contradictory in itself, as I must recognize. The fact is we must, on the one hand, try to help those tobacco producers, and also those communities that depend on them, that have grown in line with that production, that directly depend on it, and the future of which is closely linked with the performance of the tobacco industry. So the motion now before us proposes that the Standing Committee on Agriculture be empowered to study that question, through some sort of in-depth scrutiny, to derive some kind of expertise, and surely on future possibilites, on the present situation, so that we might take concrete steps to help those thousands of persons directly affected by that industry. The motion as such seems most commendable. It must be encouraged and supported, and such is the approach taken by this Party regarding this motion, as we give it our unreserved support.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   AGRICULTURE SUGGESTED STUDY OF TOBACCO GROWING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the few moments to explain the support which we will be giving to this measure. We in my Party agree that this item should go to a committee for further discussion. We do this, however, in an attempt to make it very clear that the decisions which have to be made now by the Government should in no way await any decision by that committee. There are some very clear decisions which are on the desk of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) at the moment which require immediate action if the tobacco farmers in Ontario, the Atlantic Provinces and Quebec are going to survive another year or two years.
November 21, 1985

As the House has been made aware, the tobacco farmers are under a great deal of economic pressure at the moment because the Tobacco Manufactures Council-which is in effect a very well organized oligopoly working of a few very powerful companies which have decided to work together through that Council-have organized themselves to fight the attempt by the producers to form a National Marketing Agency. The permissive legislation for that Agency was passed in this House in the fall of 1984 and the farmers have hit road-block after road-block in implementing that plan and getting it to work. The most recent road-block was a court order by one of the justices of our court system who suggested that because the cost of production formula had not been submitted to cross-examination by the tobacco manufacturers, either the process should be reinitiated or the whole thing stopped entirely. The Cabinet now has a decision to make as to whether to appeal that decision through the courts or to direct its National Farm Products Marketing Council to reinitiate the hearings concerning the cost of production Figures which are proposed in the plan. Either way, it will take some time and will probably mean that tobacco farmers will miss one more year of having the right to negotiate prices on a national basis and to have some control over imports.
That is extremely important when we look at what these 2,000 producers are up against. Over the years demand for their product has actually been holding or increasing slightly in Canada. Smoking is becoming less popular as the health effects are becoming better understood. Basically we produced some 58 billion cigarettes in the 1970s and we seem to be producing 60 billion or 61 billion cigarettes in the 1980s. Therefore the production has remained relatively stable. Yet we are told by the Tobacco Marketing Council this year that it only needs 60 million or 70 million pounds of a normal requirement of some 170 million to 180 million pounds. The proposition which is being put forward on the table indicates that the Tobacco Marketing Council is not particularly interested in this tobacco crop. The reason it is doing this is quite clear. It happens every time the farmers get the right to put forward a marketing plan. The buyers of that product do everything in their power to make certain that the plan does not get off the ground.
We have suggested to the Minister in this House that one of the ways, perhaps, he could help to ease the two parties toward the bargaining table would be to make it very clear to the Tobacco Marketing Council, the manufacturers, that if it chooses to pull out of the country-which is one of the threats it has thrown out a number of times-that brands of tobacco or products those particular companies choose to produce would no longer be permitted back into the country, for health reasons, trade reasons and a whole host of other reasons. The Minister has hesitated to make such a move. We have found that in order to make up the clearly understood shortfall of the manufacturers' production requirements in this country, they have been importing products from outside. That seems to be of concern both amongst health people and producers, perhaps for different reasons, but sometimes their interests are fairly
Tobacco Growing Industry
common. They are concerned about pesticide residue in this imported product. The tobacco growers of Ontario had written to the Minister of Agriculture asking for upgraded analyses of imported tobacco for pesticide residue content, and they received a nice reply from the Minister on November 5 which said that officers from the agriculture inspection directorate of his Department will collect the sample material and forward it to the Ontario Ministry of Agriculture and Food Pesticide Residue Laboratory at the University of Guelph for analysis. He said: "Officers of my Department will be in touch with you directly to co-ordinate their sampling activities with any special needs or interests that you may have". He had explained previously in the letter that it was a joint federal-provincial sampling agreement which was at work.
Some 10 days later another letter arrived on the subject of imported tobacco samples which came from the program officer, pesticides, Ontario region, who informed the board: "It has come to my attention that our tobacco sampling program must temporarily be put on hold. Customs officials in Ottawa have refused to provide the information required for timely sampling." We do not seem to be getting uniform messages from the federal Government with regard to this issue. The question that continues to arise is whether the Government is concerned and interested in setting up such a national program. Is it concerned about protecting producers in Canada? The actions to date are not clear, and I think that it is time that producers received a little more indication from the Minister of Agriculture, and from the Cabinet, that they are indeed serious about setting up this national agency.
This is important not only for agriculture but for consumers as well because it provides a means of monitoring the size of the crop and imports. This is an extremely important power to have in the hands of farmers when they know they are producing a commodity which has limited expansion possibilities. Without a national marketing board it will be chaos for those producers and towns and villages in tobacco producing areas. Without those powers they will not be able to restrict production in a way which will permit them to ease slowly into the production of other crops and out of tobacco. Without the protection of such an agency it will be the dog eat dog world of a big oligopoly or near monopoly picking off the smaller producers one after the other. Hundreds of tobacco producers will be forced out of business this year, several hundred next year, until the industry has shrunk to just a few producers. The producers themselves have been trying to do that in a more humane way by operating through a marketing agency to distribute the pain and permit the industry to shrink to fit the new health conscious consumers we have now.
Tobacco producers are attempting to fit their product to this new reality. As the Hon. Member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer) noted, Canadian tobacco has one of the lower tar contents of any tobacco in the world. This means it has a slightly lower carcinogen level so there is somewhat less of a chance of contracting cancer of the lungs and related diseases due to smoking. I do not want to leave the impression that Canadian

November 21, 1985
Tobacco Growing Industry
tobacco is necessarily good for you. There are 30,000 to 35,000 Canadians who die each year from tobacco-related diseases. About 5,000 of those people have not smoked but have had secondary exposure to smoke in private meeting rooms and in public places. About one-fifth to one-seventh of the people who contract cancer and related diseases are people who are not active smokers themselves. As well we have a cost to the economy each year of some $85 million in property loss due to fire started by careless smokers. Therefore, there are some very real economic and health reasons for phasing down smoking, and only a national marketing agency will permit producers to make the necessary adjustments without causing undue harm and hardship to their communities. They will be able to make the transition over a few years rather than having to decide whether they go bankrupt next year or not.
I hope that when this proposal goes to committee the committee's work will encompass not only production and marketing problems, and the shenanigans going on between growers and processors, but that it will also spend a considerable amount of time on the health effects of the use of tobacco. I hope it will look at possible changes to the tax laws which will have an impact both on the growers and users of tobacco.
The committee should also look at the use of tobacco advertising. From the roughly $300 million of product that the farmer sells there is generated just over $2 billion of economic activity through processing, taxing and advertising of tobacco products. Advertising is a very large part of that $2 billion. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has just begun an anti-smoking advertising campaign. It is a very small campaign and we should be looking at proposals to change the tax laws as they apply to advertising. Perhaps it is time to look at a system for reducing the amount of advertising dollars which can be claimed as legitimate expenses for tax purposes by tobacco companies. Perhaps we should place a surtax on advertising to raise money to produce a counteradvertising campaign as well as providing assistance to producers to get into new forms of agricultural production. These are some things the committee should look at when it sets out its terms of reference. I hope the committee is able to follow in the footsteps of the Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer (Mr. Isabelle) who produced the report on tobacco and a part of the industry in 1971 and presented it to this House at that time. It is time to review the industry from production to final use, to look at the health effects, and look at a means of marketing which will permit producers to adjust to the new realities.
Because my time is nearly up and I am putting you to sleep, Mr. Speaker, I think we should stop at this point, vote on the proposal, which I understand will receive unanimous approval, and send it off to the appropriate committee.
