speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take advantage of this opportunity to raise a question which I feel is very important, in the circumstances.
The previous Member for Lotbiniere, Mr. Speaker, was probably one of the most forceful defenders of the agri-food industry in recent years. He represented a riding where farming is the major industry, as it is in Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot and Drummondville, and the Member in question, and I am referring to Mr. Jean-Guy Dubois, worked very hard for the implementation of a project that was to be set up in his riding, at Victoriaville.
I am referring to the plant protection laboratory that was to be established for the purpose of enforcing the Plant Quarantine Act. It was a project worth $13 million, of which $12 million was to be financed from the Laprade Fund and $1 million from public funds allocated under the budget for Agriculture Canada.
The project was officially announced on June 13, 1984, and this announcement was followed by an Order in Council on July 11, 1984-I can even give the House the number: 794586-which made the project official.
The project as such would have had and was supposed to have a very positive impact on this farming district. I saw it as a sign that the agricultural industry in this riding, and in Saint-Hyacinthe and Lennoxville where other laboratories were set up, had attained the status it deserved. During the election campaign, the project was frequently discussed, and the present Member made a firm commitment that the project would be implemented in the weeks following his election. Surprisingly, today it is November 21, so it was a year ago on September 4, when I put a question recently to the Minister, the Hon. Minister for Agriculture (Mr. Wise) answered, and I quote: "Mr. Speaker, I regret that 1 do not
November 21, 1985

have sufficient information to respond specifically about the project to which the Hon. Member refers. I am very happy to take notice of the question and will get back to the Hon. Member."
This was not a project worth $30,000, $35,000 or $50,000, Mr. Speaker. This was a project worth $13 million with spinoffs in terms of very good jobs for 50 technicians and 15 scientists, not to mention the supporting staff and all the indirect benefits .. . This is a project worth $13 million, and all the Minister of Agriculture can reply is this: I do not know. I do not have the information.
Mr. Speaker, this makes me wonder about what the present Hon. Member has been doing for his riding. Instead of coming to my riding and telling my constituents that the federal Government would richly subsidize industrial motels, which is not the case, I think that he should limit himself to defending the interests of his riding and make the necessary representations to his Minister, because it seems to me totally unacceptable that the Minister of Agriculture should not be aware of a project worth $13 million which had been planned for Vic-toriaville.
There had been an announcement. The Treasury Board had approved the expenditures and civil servants had even taken steps to find the proper site. Now, a year and a few months after this announcement, the Minister makes the following statement: I do not know what it is all about. I am going to find out and get back to the Hon. Member in due course.
This is an insult to a great many people who have been waiting for this project and are dependent upon it being carried out. Under the previous administration, we had put together two projects which I felt had extremely important benefits. There was the Mapping Centre in Sherbrooke and the Plant Health Centre in Victoriaville. These were two regional projects which would have established the economic importance of the greater Eastern Townships and Bois-Francs area. And of those two projects, one is being questioned and the other one is unknown in Ottawa.
I think that under the circumstances, I am not being petty when I ask myself certain questions and when I say that I have some reservations about what has been done, because if I had a $13 million project for my riding, you can be sure, Mr. Speaker, that I would harass the Minister, I would raise the matter with him day after day until a final decision is reached. Will it be built or not?
Mir. Pierre Blais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture): Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) cannot be faulted for not responding immediately when the question was put to him on October 31. As Hon. Members know, when specific questions are raised during oral questions period, Mr. Speaker himself does not
Adjournment Debate
usually allow five- or ten-minute answers to any given question.
So the Minister simply said that he would eventually get back to the Hon. Member, and we now have the opportunity to do so this evening.
As the Hon. Member would know, the Minister of Agriculture reviews his programs on a regular basis to make sure they are still appropriate and meet the requirements of the industries for which they are designed.
One of the programs under active consideration has to do with the protection of vegetables and related quarantine facilities. The mandate of the Department is to prevent the introduction and spreading of agents which might be harmful to the production and marketing of plants and their products. We must also ensure that all farm and forest products likely to harbour phytoparasites meet the quarantine standards of importing countries.
The departmental study committee includes representatives from the private sector. That sector does not act lightly. Canada's achievements in that sector are highly esteemed everywhere, and it is my view that we must maintain that high level of quality.
The number and the location of inspection points for crops under plant quarantine are included in the list of problems identified by the comittee, Mr. Speaker.
The committee also looks into the way the program's scientific support services are distributed to optimize the ratio of inspection and program staff to the scientific support staff. This is something not to be done lightly. I appreciate that as a crash action, the previous Government, perhaps to get the support of people in that area, wanted to announce a project to get votes. That may have been so, but people were not misled.
There is also a sub-committee that is now looking into how and where this project is to be undertaken.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, we took specific measures to make sure that the right location is chosen. Consider also the fact that the site which had been selected and which still has not been rejected up until now, gave rise within that very committee and within the private sector itself, to certain difficulties linked with its remoteness with respect to transportation, from some areas. This was not raised by us but by the private sector, which you have a duty to represent, as I do, and as does each and every Member in this House.
In view of the fact that this Government is also making every effort to control its expenditures, something the previous Government was not doing . . . They found it easy to announce projects, because with a running deficit that had reached $200 billion, $13 million did not make that much difference. But this is not the way we-
The private sector is asked to invest, the Government joins in, perhaps not to the least possible extent, but still it must join

in so that projects are carried out, but it is not the Government's role to always assume the financial responsibility for all those projects.
Mr. Speaker, that project should ... by the end of the fiscal year, we will have a final answer concerning the location of that centre.
